relation_operation__composition.title: Relation composition and intermediate elements
relation_operation__composition.summary: Relation composition joins two links through the same intermediate element.
relation_operation__composition.definition: For R⊆A×B and S⊆B×C, S∘R here means first R, then S: (a,c)∈S∘R if and only if there exists b∈B such that aRb and bSc.
relation_operation__composition.explanation: The existential condition means that even if several intermediate elements realize the same endpoint pair, that pair appears only once. Composition is associative and distributes over relation union, but is generally not commutative. In relation matrices, multiplication uses AND and summation uses OR.
notation: a(S∘R)c ⇔ there exists b such that aRb and bSc.
R∘I_A=R and I_B∘R=R, with types understood as a relation R:A→B.
relation_operation__composition.example: User Alpha belongs to the readers group, and the readers group may read a document. Composing group membership with group resource permissions shows that Alpha may read the document.
common_mistakes: Executing the relation on the right last.
Treating values greater than 1 from ordinary matrix multiplication as repeated elements of a relation.

relation_operation__inverse_relation.title: Inverse relations and their laws
relation_operation__inverse_relation.summary: An inverse relation swaps the two components of each ordered pair; it does not take a complement.
relation_operation__inverse_relation.definition: For R⊆A×B, define R⁻¹={(b,a)｜(a,b)∈R}, a relation from B to A. The inverse of a general relation need not be a function.
relation_operation__inverse_relation.explanation: Taking the inverse twice recovers the original relation. Inversion respects union and intersection of relations of the same type. In a directed graph it reverses every edge; loops remain loops. In matrix form it is transposition. Inverting a composition reverses the order of composition.
notation: (R⁻¹)⁻¹=R.
(R∪S)⁻¹=R⁻¹∪S⁻¹; (R∩S)⁻¹=R⁻¹∩S⁻¹.
relation_operation__inverse_relation.example: The inverse of R={(1,a),(2,a)} is {(a,1),(a,2)}. Since a has two associated values, this is not a function from {a} to {1,2}.
common_mistakes: Confusing the inverse with the complement obtained by removing the original relation.
Keeping the original row and column object types after inversion.

relation_operation__powers.title: Relation powers and chains of fixed length
relation_operation__powers.summary: The kth power of a relation describes which endpoints are reachable in exactly k steps.
relation_operation__powers.definition: For a relation R on A, R⁰=I_A and R^(k+1)=R∘R^k. For a positive integer k, (x,y)∈R^k means that a chain of k R-edges connects x to y; repeated vertices and edges are allowed.
relation_operation__powers.explanation: A power records whether an endpoint pair is reachable, not the number of chains realizing it. A finite chain with no continuation can eventually have empty higher powers. Directed cycles give periodic behavior in the lengths and can produce diagonal pairs in positive powers.
notation: R¹=R; R⁰ is independent of whether R has loops.
R^m∘R^n=R^(m+n) for nonnegative integers m,n.
relation_operation__powers.example: The directed 3-cycle 0→1→2→0 satisfies R³=I_A and R⁴=R.
common_mistakes: Interpreting R² as numerically squaring each edge.
Requiring a fixed-length relation chain to be a simple path with no repeated vertices.

relation_operation__set_operations.title: Union, intersection, and difference of relations
relation_operation__set_operations.summary: Relations of the same type admit ordinary set operations on ordered pairs.
relation_operation__set_operations.definition: For R,S⊆A×B, R∪S, R∩S, and R\S consist respectively of pairs appearing in at least one relation, in both relations, and in R only.
relation_operation__set_operations.explanation: The result is still a relation from A to B. Union permits either set of rules, while intersection requires both sets of rules to permit a pair. Composition distributes over union, but for intersection only an inclusion generally holds; distribution cannot be assumed.
notation: T∘(R∩S)⊆(T∘R)∩(T∘S); the reverse inclusion generally fails.
relation_operation__set_operations.example: If R={(1,a)} and S={(1,b)}, then R∩S=∅ and R∪S={(1,a),(1,b)}.
common_mistakes: Confusing intersection with joining two successive relations.
Applying the distributive law for union directly to intersection.

relation_property.title: Properties of relations
relation_property.summary: Relation properties are universal conditions; check diagonals, edges in both directions, and two-step chains carefully.
relation_property.definition: For a relation R on A: reflexive means aRa for every a∈A; irreflexive means not aRa for every a; symmetric means aRb implies bRa; antisymmetric means aRb and bRa imply a=b; transitive means aRb and bRc imply aRc.
relation_property.explanation: Symmetry and antisymmetry are not logical negations. A relation containing only diagonal pairs may satisfy both. A relation with a bidirectional pair of distinct elements and another edge lacking its reverse may satisfy neither. Properties must be checked relative to the specified set A. On nonempty A, for example, the empty relation is not reflexive but is irreflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive. If A=∅, all these universal conditions hold.
notation: aRb means (a,b)∈R.
Reflexivity requires every diagonal pair; irreflexivity excludes every diagonal pair.
Antisymmetry only forbids edges in both directions between distinct elements.
relation_property.example: On A={1,2,3}, R={(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)} is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, but not antisymmetric, since 1≠2 while 1R2 and 2R1.
common_mistakes: Interpreting antisymmetric as having no symmetric ordered pairs at all.
Checking transitivity only on distinct elements and missing diagonals required by bidirectional edges.
Treating a false antecedent with no counterexample as a failure of the property.

relation_property__antisymmetry.title: Antisymmetric relations
relation_property__antisymmetry.summary: Antisymmetry forbids bidirectional links between distinct objects.
relation_property__antisymmetry.definition: R on A is antisymmetric if aRb and bRa imply a=b; equivalently, R∩R⁻¹⊆I_A.
relation_property__antisymmetry.explanation: Antisymmetry allows loops and one-way links between distinct objects. It is neither incompatible with symmetry nor its negation: every subrelation of the diagonal satisfies both, whereas a relation with a bidirectional edge and another edge lacking its reverse satisfies neither.
notation: If a≠b, aRb and bRa cannot both hold.
R is both symmetric and antisymmetric ⇔ R⊆I_A.
relation_property__antisymmetry.example: The relation ≤ on integers is antisymmetric and contains every loop; {(1,2),(2,1)} is not antisymmetric when 1≠2.
common_mistakes: Declaring a relation non-antisymmetric because it has a loop.
Thinking every edge, including a loop, must lack a reverse.

relation_property__irreflexivity.title: Irreflexive relations
relation_property__irreflexivity.summary: Irreflexivity excludes every link from an object to itself.
relation_property__irreflexivity.definition: A relation R on A is irreflexive if (a,a)∉R for every a∈A, that is, R∩I_A=∅.
relation_property__irreflexivity.explanation: Failure of reflexivity requires just one missing loop, whereas irreflexivity requires all loops to be absent. These are different conditions. On nonempty A, reflexivity and irreflexivity are incompatible, but both may fail; on empty A both hold.
notation: Irreflexive: ∀a∈A, ¬aRa.
Not reflexive: there exists a∈A such that ¬aRa.
relation_property__irreflexivity.example: On A={1,2}, {(1,2)} is irreflexive; {(1,1)} is neither reflexive nor irreflexive.
common_mistakes: Equating not reflexive with irreflexive.
Checking one loop-free object and concluding irreflexivity.

relation_property__reflexivity.title: Reflexive relations
relation_property__reflexivity.summary: Reflexivity requires every object to be related to itself.
relation_property__reflexivity.definition: A relation R on A is reflexive if (a,a)∈R for every a∈A, equivalently I_A⊆R.
relation_property__reflexivity.explanation: All diagonal pairs must be checked relative to the specified A; finding one loop is insufficient. When A=∅, the empty relation is reflexive because there is no element violating the universal condition. Enlarging the underlying set without changing the relation may make a previously reflexive relation nonreflexive.
notation: Reflexive: ∀a∈A, aRa.
relation_property__reflexivity.example: For A={1,2,3}, {(1,1),(2,2)} is not reflexive because (3,3) is missing.
common_mistakes: Checking only objects that appear in the relation.
Inferring from failure of reflexivity that no diagonal pairs exist.

relation_property__symmetry.title: Symmetric relations
relation_property__symmetry.summary: Symmetry requires a reverse link for every link.
relation_property__symmetry.definition: A relation R on A is symmetric if, for any a,b∈A, aRb implies bRa. Equivalently, R=R⁻¹.
relation_property__symmetry.explanation: A loop automatically satisfies its own reverse requirement. The empty relation and any relation consisting only of diagonal pairs are symmetric. To disprove symmetry, find an existing edge whose reverse is missing; finding two unrelated objects is insufficient.
notation: ∀a,b, aRb⇒bRa.
R∪R⁻¹ is always symmetric.
relation_property__symmetry.example: R={(1,2),(2,1),(3,3)} is symmetric. Adding (2,3) without adding (3,2) destroys symmetry.
common_mistakes: Thinking a relation with no edges cannot be symmetric.
Treating antisymmetry as the logical negation of symmetry.

relation_property__transitivity.title: Transitivity and the two-step test
relation_property__transitivity.summary: Transitivity requires a direct link between the endpoints of every two-step relation chain.
relation_property__transitivity.definition: R is transitive if for all a,b,c∈A, aRb and bRc imply aRc. The elements a,b,c need not be distinct.
relation_property__transitivity.explanation: Under the right-to-left composition convention used here, transitivity is equivalent to R∘R⊆R. A relation with no composable edges is still transitive because no failing instance exists. Even when R and S are separately transitive, their union need not be: edges from the two relations may create new two-step chains.
notation: R²⊆R expresses transitivity in relation algebra.
If aRb and bRa, transitivity also requires aRa and bRb.
relation_property__transitivity.example: {(1,2),(2,1)} is not transitive because (1,1) and (2,2) are missing, even though it has no three distinct vertices.
common_mistakes: Checking only chains of three distinct elements.
Declaring a relation nontransitive because it has no two-step chains.

relation_equivalence.title: Equivalence relations and partitions
relation_equivalence.summary: An equivalence relation divides a set into disjoint equivalence classes forming a partition.
relation_equivalence.definition: A relation on A is an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. The equivalence class of a is [a]_R={x∈A｜xRa}. A partition of A is a family of nonempty subsets that are pairwise disjoint and have union A; the partition of the empty set is the empty family.
relation_equivalence.explanation: Distinct equivalence classes are disjoint, and every element belongs to exactly one class. Conversely, declaring elements related when they belong to the same partition block gives an equivalence relation. These constructions correspond to each other. For a finite set with block sizes n₁,…,n_k, the relation has n₁²+…+n_k² ordered pairs, rather than the number of blocks or elements.
notation: [a]_R denotes the class of a; A/R denotes the quotient set of all classes.
aRb ⇔ [a]_R=[b]_R.
Congruence a≡b (mod m) means m divides a−b, where m is a positive integer.
relation_equivalence.example: On {0,1,2,3,4,5}, congruence modulo 3 gives the three classes {0,3}, {1,4}, {2,5}. The corresponding relation contains 3×2²=12 ordered pairs.
common_mistakes: Confusing the number of classes with the number of ordered pairs in the relation.
Allowing empty or overlapping blocks or omitting elements from a partition.
Counting the same class repeatedly because its representatives differ.

relation_equivalence__classes.title: Equivalence classes
relation_equivalence__classes.summary: An equivalence class contains every object equivalent to a representative.
relation_equivalence__classes.definition: Let R be an equivalence relation on A. For a∈A, define [a]_R={x∈A｜xRa}. Two equivalence classes are either equal or disjoint.
relation_equivalence__classes.explanation: Reflexivity ensures a∈[a]. If aRb, symmetry and transitivity prove [a]=[b], so different representatives within one class do not give different classes. For finite class sizes n_i, the relation has size Σn_i².
notation: aRb ⇔ [a]_R=[b]_R.
relation_equivalence__classes.example: Congruence modulo 3 on {0,…,8} has three classes: {0,3,6}, {1,4,7}, {2,5,8}.
common_mistakes: Counting representatives instead of distinct classes.
Forgetting each element's self-relation within a class.

relation_equivalence__partitions.title: The correspondence between partitions and equivalence relations
relation_equivalence__partitions.summary: Partitions and equivalence relations describe the same classification structure in two ways.
relation_equivalence__partitions.definition: A partition of A is a family of nonempty, pairwise disjoint blocks whose union is A. Given a partition, relating two elements exactly when they are in the same block defines an equivalence relation on A.
relation_equivalence__partitions.explanation: Every element must lie in exactly one block. Taking classes of the relation generated by a partition recovers its blocks; the reverse construction also works. The partition of the empty set is the empty family, consistent with requiring every block to be nonempty.
notation: For a partition {B_i}, the corresponding relation is R=⋃_i(B_i×B_i).
For block sizes n_i, |R|=Σn_i².
relation_equivalence__partitions.example: {{1,3},{2,4,5}} partitions {1,2,3,4,5}. Its relation contains both directions between 4 and 5, but no link from 1 to 2.
common_mistakes: Allowing partition blocks to overlap or omit objects.
Including an empty block in a partition.

relation_equivalence__quotient_refinemen.title: Partition refinement and the natural quotient map
relation_equivalence__quotient_refinemen.summary: Every block of a finer partition lies in a block of a coarser partition.
relation_equivalence__quotient_refinemen.definition: For equivalence relations R,S on the same set, R⊆S is equivalent to every R-class being contained in an S-class. The partition of R is then finer than that of S, and there is a natural map [a]_R↦[a]_S.
relation_equivalence__quotient_refinemen.explanation: The natural map is well-defined because R-equivalent representatives are necessarily S-equivalent. It is always surjective, but distinct finer classes may merge, so it need not be injective. A larger relation has more links and hence coarser classes, possibly fewer of them.
notation: R⊆S ⇔ [a]_R⊆[a]_S for every a.
The natural map has type A/R→A/S.
relation_equivalence__quotient_refinemen.example: Classification modulo 4 refines classification modulo 2: the classes of 0 and 2 modulo 4 both map to the even class modulo 2.
common_mistakes: Reversing the direction between refinement and relation inclusion.
Defining a map on a quotient without checking independence of the representative.

relation_equivalence__quotient_set.title: Quotient sets
relation_equivalence__quotient_set.summary: A quotient set treats each entire equivalence class as a new element.
relation_equivalence__quotient_set.definition: For an equivalence relation R on A, the quotient set is A/R={[a]_R｜a∈A}. Its elements are the distinct equivalence classes, rather than their representatives.
relation_equivalence__quotient_set.explanation: The natural projection π:A→A/R, π(a)=[a]_R, is surjective. In the finite case, the quotient's size is the number of partition blocks, not the number of ordered pairs in the relation, and need not equal the number of representatives. The quotient of the empty set is empty.
notation: π(a)=π(b) if and only if aRb.
|A/R| is the number of distinct equivalence classes.
relation_equivalence__quotient_set.example: For congruence modulo 3 on the integers, the three elements of Z/R may be written [0], [1], [2]; each is itself an infinite set.
common_mistakes: Writing a quotient as an arbitrary set of representatives without explaining the identification.
Using the number of ordered pairs as the quotient's size.

relation_order.title: Partial orders
relation_order.summary: Partial orders allow incomparable elements; minimal versus least and maximal versus greatest must be distinguished.
relation_order.definition: A reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation on A is a partial order, written ≤. If every two elements are comparable, it is a total order. For a subset S, a∈S is minimal if no element of S is strictly less than a; a∈S is least if a is less than or equal to every element of S. Maximal and greatest elements are defined dually and must also belong to S.
relation_order.explanation: A least element, if it exists, is unique and minimal. There may be several minimal elements, and a minimal element need not be comparable to the others. An upper bound of S is an element of the ambient poset A greater than or equal to every element of S; it need not belong to S. The least upper bound is the least of all upper bounds; greatest lower bounds are defined dually. A finite poset's Hasse diagram shows only covers, omitting loops and edges implied by transitivity. In a finite nonempty poset, following a strictly descending chain reaches a minimal element.
notation: a<b means a≤b and a≠b.
b covers a if a<b and there is no c with a<c<b.
Divisibility a|b and numerical order ≤ are different relations.
relation_order.example: In {1,2,3,6} ordered by divisibility, 1 is least and 6 is greatest; 2 and 3 are incomparable. The covers are 1→2, 1→3, 2→6, 3→6.
common_mistakes: Using vertical positions in a Hasse diagram alone to prove comparability.
Confusing least with minimal or greatest with maximal.
Using an element outside the given poset as a least upper or greatest lower bound.

relation_order__greatest.title: Greatest elements
relation_order__greatest.summary: A greatest element is greater than or equal to every element of its subset.
relation_order__greatest.definition: For a subset S of a poset A, m∈S is a greatest element if s≤m for every s∈S.
relation_order__greatest.explanation: A greatest element, if present, is unique and maximal; multiple maximal elements rule out a greatest element. Even if the whole poset has a greatest element, a subset may omit it and have no greatest element of its own.
notation: m=max S requires m∈S and ∀s∈S, s≤m.
A greatest element is also the least upper bound of S.
relation_order__greatest.example: In {1,2,3,6,12} ordered by divisibility, 12 is the greatest element.
common_mistakes: Immediately identifying a maximal element as greatest.
Using the ambient set's greatest element for a subset that does not contain it.

relation_order__hasse_diagram.title: Covers and Hasse diagrams
relation_order__hasse_diagram.summary: A finite poset's Hasse diagram shows only covers and uses height for direction.
relation_order__hasse_diagram.definition: In a finite poset, b covers a if a<b and no c satisfies a<c<b. A Hasse diagram uses vertices for elements, omits loops and edges forced by transitivity, and joins only covering pairs, with the greater element higher.
relation_order__hasse_diagram.explanation: In a finite Hasse diagram, two distinct elements are comparable exactly when an upward chain of covers connects them. No direct edge does not imply incomparability, since an indirect upward chain may exist. Positions may be adjusted while preserving cover directions. For general infinite posets, the cover graph alone may not recover the order; for example, the usual order on the rationals has no covers.
notation: a≺b often means b covers a; specify the convention first.
Hasse diagram edges are not all ordered pairs of the partial order.
relation_order__hasse_diagram.example: The divisibility Hasse diagram of {1,2,3,6} has edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–6, 3–6; it omits 1–6.
common_mistakes: Retaining every transitive edge and cluttering the diagram.
Concluding incomparability from the absence of a direct edge.

relation_order__infimum.title: Greatest lower bounds (infima)
relation_order__infimum.summary: The infimum is the greatest of all lower bounds.
relation_order__infimum.definition: If l is a lower bound of S and every lower bound v of S satisfies v≤l, then l is the greatest lower bound, written inf S.
relation_order__infimum.explanation: An infimum, if present, is unique but need not belong to S. In a power set ordered by inclusion it is given by intersection. In a given divisibility poset, even a computable integer gcd must belong to the ambient set to serve as an infimum.
notation: inf S=max L(S), provided this greatest element exists.
If min S exists, inf S=min S.
relation_order__infimum.example: In P({a,b,c}), the infimum of {{a},{b}} is ∅.
common_mistakes: Confusing a maximal lower bound with the greatest lower bound.
Using a gcd outside the ambient set as an infimum.

relation_order__least.title: Least elements
relation_order__least.summary: A least element is less than or equal to every element of its subset.
relation_order__least.definition: For a subset S of a poset A, m∈S is least if m≤s for every s∈S.
relation_order__least.explanation: A least element, if present, is unique and minimal. The converse does not hold in general. In a finite nonempty poset with a unique minimal element, every element descends to it, so it is least.
notation: m=min S requires both m∈S and ∀s∈S, m≤s.
A least element is also the greatest lower bound of S.
relation_order__least.example: In {1,2,3,6} ordered by divisibility, 1 is least; removing 1 can leave multiple minimal elements.
common_mistakes: Calling a chosen minimal element least.
Choosing a least element outside the given subset.

relation_order__linear_extension.title: Linear extensions of partial orders
relation_order__linear_extension.summary: A linear extension orders incomparable elements while preserving existing order constraints.
relation_order__linear_extension.definition: A linear extension of a poset (A,≤) is a total order ≤_L on the same A such that a≤b implies a≤_L b. In the finite case it can be described by a permutation satisfying every strict precedence constraint.
relation_order__linear_extension.explanation: A linear extension never reverses an established comparison; it chooses orders only for undecided pairs. Different topological sorts of a finite poset correspond to different linear extensions. Incomparable pairs affect the number of allowable permutations, but their directions cannot be chosen independently while ignoring transitivity.
notation: If a<b, a must appear before b in the permutation.
relation_order__linear_extension.example: The divisibility poset {1,2,3,6} has two linear extensions: 1,2,3,6 and 1,3,2,6.
common_mistakes: Freely swapping comparable elements.
Multiplying two choices for each incomparable pair while ignoring transitivity constraints.

relation_order__lower_bound.title: Lower bounds
relation_order__lower_bound.summary: A lower bound must belong to the given poset and be no greater than any element of the subset.
relation_order__lower_bound.definition: For a subset S of a poset (A,≤), l∈A is a lower bound of S if l≤s for every s∈S.
relation_order__lower_bound.explanation: A lower bound may lie outside S, and there may be none. In divisibility order, lower bounds are common divisors belonging to the ambient A; 1 cannot be included unconditionally. Every ambient element is a lower bound of the empty subset.
notation: L(S)={l∈A｜∀s∈S, l≤s} is the set of lower bounds.
A least element, if present, is a lower bound.
relation_order__lower_bound.example: For A={2,3,6,12,18} and S={2,3} ordered by divisibility, S has no lower bound: its only positive common divisor, 1, is outside A.
common_mistakes: Treating an integer common divisor as an element of the current poset.
Confusing a subset's least element with a lower bound in the ambient set.

relation_order__maximal.title: Maximal elements
relation_order__maximal.summary: A maximal element only excludes strictly greater elements in its subset.
relation_order__maximal.definition: For a subset S of a poset A, m∈S is maximal if there is no s∈S with m<s.
relation_order__maximal.explanation: A maximal element may be incomparable with others and therefore need not be greatest. Every finite nonempty poset has a maximal element and may have several. Maximal and minimal elements are dual under reversal of the order.
notation: Maximal: no s∈S satisfies m≤s and s≠m.
A maximal element must belong to S.
relation_order__maximal.example: In {2,3,6,10} ordered by divisibility, both 6 and 10 are maximal, but no greatest element exists.
common_mistakes: Interpreting no greater element as greater than or equal to everyone.
Missing multiple incomparable maximal elements.

relation_order__minimal.title: Minimal elements
relation_order__minimal.summary: A minimal element only requires the absence of a strictly smaller element in its subset.
relation_order__minimal.definition: For a subset S of a poset A, m∈S is minimal if no s∈S satisfies s<m.
relation_order__minimal.explanation: Minimality does not guarantee comparability with every other element, so several minimal elements may exist. Every finite nonempty poset has a minimal element. An infinite poset may have none, or have a unique minimal element without a least element.
notation: Minimal: no s∈S satisfies s≤m and s≠m.
A minimal element must belong to S.
relation_order__minimal.example: In {2,3,6,10} ordered by divisibility, both 2 and 3 are minimal.
common_mistakes: Equating minimal with least.
Applying the finite result that a unique minimal element is least to infinite posets.

relation_order__partial_order.title: Nonstrict partial orders
relation_order__partial_order.summary: Reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity describe consistent nonstrict comparison.
relation_order__partial_order.definition: A nonstrict partial order ≤ on A is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation. (A,≤) is called a poset. It need not make every two elements comparable.
relation_order__partial_order.explanation: Set inclusion and divisibility of positive integers are partial orders. Distinct elements with neither a≤b nor b≤a are incomparable. The strict relation a<b is defined by a≤b and a≠b; do not mix it with the reflexive nonstrict definition.
notation: Reflexivity, antisymmetry, and transitivity are all required.
a∥b often denotes incomparability; declare this convention when using it.
relation_order__partial_order.example: In {1,2,3,6} ordered by divisibility, 2 and 3 are incomparable.
common_mistakes: Treating antisymmetry as the negation of symmetry.
Thinking a partial order must order every pair of elements.

relation_order__supremum.title: Least upper bounds (suprema)
relation_order__supremum.summary: A supremum is the least upper bound, not just any minimal upper bound.
relation_order__supremum.definition: If u is an upper bound of S and u≤v for every upper bound v of S, then u is the least upper bound, written sup S.
relation_order__supremum.explanation: A supremum, if present, is unique but need not belong to S. In a power set ordered by inclusion, sup{A_i}=⋃A_i. An upper bound that is merely minimal but incomparable with another upper bound cannot be called the least upper bound on that basis.
notation: sup S=min U(S), provided this least element exists.
If max S exists, sup S=max S.
relation_order__supremum.example: In P({a,b,c}), {{a},{b}} has supremum {a,b}, which is not a member of this two-element subset.
common_mistakes: Calling an arbitrary upper bound or minimal upper bound the supremum.
Requiring the supremum to belong to the original subset.

relation_order__total_order.title: Total orders and comparability
relation_order__total_order.summary: A total order is a partial order in which every two elements are comparable.
relation_order__total_order.definition: A partial order ≤ is total if for all a,b∈A, a≤b or b≤a. A totally ordered subset is also called a chain.
relation_order__total_order.explanation: First establish a partial order, then check comparability of every pair. Lexicographic order prioritizes the first component; it differs from componentwise comparison, which generally has incomparable pairs.
notation: Total order⇒partial order, but a partial order need not be total.
Comparability allows a=b.
relation_order__total_order.example: Divisibility restricted to {1,2,4,8} is a total order, but restricted to {1,2,3,6} it is not.
common_mistakes: Inferring a total order solely from vertical placement in a diagram.
Checking only some pairs and concluding all are comparable.

relation_order__upper_bound.title: Upper bounds
relation_order__upper_bound.summary: An upper bound compares with every element of the subset but need only belong to the ambient poset.
relation_order__upper_bound.definition: For a subset S of a poset (A,≤), u∈A is an upper bound of S if s≤u for every s∈S.
relation_order__upper_bound.explanation: An upper bound need not belong to S or be unique. Fix the ambient A before finding bounds: an upper bound in a larger set may not belong to the current A. Every ambient element is an upper bound of the empty subset.
notation: U(S)={u∈A｜∀s∈S, s≤u} is the set of upper bounds.
A greatest element, if present, is an upper bound; the converse fails.
relation_order__upper_bound.example: In A={2,3,6,12,18} ordered by divisibility, the upper bounds of S={2,3} are 6,12,18.
common_mistakes: Requiring every upper bound to lie in S.
Forgetting to exclude candidates outside A.

relation_closure.title: Relation closures
relation_closure.summary: A closure is the smallest relation containing the original relation and satisfying a specified property.
relation_closure.definition: For R on A, a closure with respect to a property contains R, satisfies the property, and is least under set inclusion. The reflexive closure is R∪I_A; the symmetric closure is R∪R⁻¹; the transitive closure is R⁺=R∪R²∪R³∪…; the reflexive transitive closure is R*=I_A∪R⁺.
relation_closure.explanation: The transitive closure collects endpoint pairs reachable by positive-length chains. Cycles can therefore add diagonal pairs, but isolated elements' diagonals do not automatically enter R⁺. The equivalence closure can be obtained by making every edge bidirectional, then adding pairs reachable in zero or any positive number of steps: (R∪R⁻¹)*. Leastness means each added pair is forced by the target property. Exhibiting a qualifying relation containing R does not alone prove it is the closure. Finite transitive closures can be computed by Warshall's Boolean matrix algorithm.
notation: R* and R⁺ differ in whether all diagonal pairs are included unconditionally.
The classes of the equivalence closure are the connected components obtained by ignoring directions in the original relation.
common_mistakes: Confusing transitive and reflexive transitive closures and unconditionally adding every loop.
Adding only one round of two-step links and missing pairs forced by longer chains.
Checking the property without proving that every qualifying superrelation must contain the result.

relation_closure__equivalence_closure.title: Equivalence closure and undirected connected components
relation_closure__equivalence_closure.summary: Generating the least equivalence relation requires bidirectional, transitive, and self-links.
relation_closure__equivalence_closure.definition: The equivalence closure of R is (R∪R⁻¹)*, where * denotes reflexive transitive closure. It is the least equivalence relation containing R.
relation_closure__equivalence_closure.explanation: After ignoring the original directions, all elements in the same undirected connected component must be equivalent. No links between distinct components are forced. Each isolated vertex forms its own class and must be included. For finite component sizes n_i, the closure has size Σn_i².
notation: First make edges bidirectional, then compute reachability allowing zero steps.
An isolated vertex forms a class of size 1 and contributes one diagonal pair.
relation_closure__equivalence_closure.example: For A={a,b,c,d}, R={(a,b),(b,c)}, the equivalence closure has classes {a,b,c} and {d}, hence 9+1=10 ordered pairs.
common_mistakes: Computing only transitive closure without ensuring symmetry and reflexivity.
Finding components only among vertices occurring on edges and omitting isolated vertices.

relation_closure__reflexive_closure.title: Reflexive closure
relation_closure__reflexive_closure.summary: Reflexive closure adds only missing diagonal pairs.
relation_closure__reflexive_closure.definition: The reflexive closure of R⊆A×A is r(R)=R∪I_A, the least reflexive relation containing R.
relation_closure__reflexive_closure.explanation: Leastness means adding only the loops required for reflexivity and leaving other edges as they are. Every reflexive relation containing R must contain I_A and thus R∪I_A. Existing loops are not counted twice.
notation: r(R)\R=I_A\R.
relation_closure__reflexive_closure.example: For A={1,2} and R={(1,2)}, the reflexive closure is {(1,1),(2,2),(1,2)}.
common_mistakes: Also adding reverse off-diagonal edges.
Counting an existing loop again as a new pair.

relation_closure__reflexive_transitive_c.title: Reflexive transitive closure
relation_closure__reflexive_transitive_c.summary: Star closure combines reachability in zero steps with reachability in positive steps.
relation_closure__reflexive_transitive_c.definition: The reflexive transitive closure of R is R*=I_A∪R⁺=⋃_{k≥0}R^k, the least reflexive and transitive relation containing R.
relation_closure__reflexive_transitive_c.explanation: R⁺ does not automatically include all loops, whereas R* always contains I_A. Zero-step reachability provides self-links even at sinks or isolated vertices of a finite graph. Vertices on closed walks already have self-links in R⁺.
notation: R⁰=I_A; R*=I_A∪R⁺.
If R=∅, then R⁺=∅ while R*=I_A.
relation_closure__reflexive_transitive_c.example: For the chain 1→2→3, R* contains the two original edges, 1→3, and three diagonal pairs: 6 pairs in total.
common_mistakes: Using R* and R⁺ interchangeably.
Thinking a vertex without outgoing edges cannot reach itself in star closure.

relation_closure__symmetric_closure.title: Symmetric closure
relation_closure__symmetric_closure.summary: Symmetric closure adds each edge's missing reverse.
relation_closure__symmetric_closure.definition: The symmetric closure of R is s(R)=R∪R⁻¹, the least symmetric relation containing R.
relation_closure__symmetric_closure.explanation: A loop is its own reverse, so symmetric closure does not unconditionally add loops. Existing bidirectional edges do not add new elements either. Reflexive and symmetric closure commute, but this does not imply that arbitrary closures commute.
notation: s(r(R))=r(s(R))=R∪R⁻¹∪I_A.
relation_closure__symmetric_closure.example: For A={1,2,3}, R={(1,2)}, the symmetric closure is only {(1,2),(2,1)}, with no loops.
common_mistakes: Confusing symmetric closure with equivalence closure.
Reversing edges while deleting the originals.

relation_closure__transitive_closure.title: Transitive closure, reachability, and Warshall's algorithm
relation_closure__transitive_closure.summary: Transitive closure collects endpoints reachable by positive-length chains without automatically adding all loops.
relation_closure__transitive_closure.definition: The transitive closure R⁺=⋃_{k≥1}R^k is the least transitive relation containing R; the reflexive transitive closure is R*=I_A∪R⁺. For finite relations, Warshall's algorithm computes reachability by allowing each vertex in turn as an intermediate vertex.
relation_closure__transitive_closure.explanation: Warshall's Boolean update is T[i,j]←T[i,j]∨(T[i,k]∧T[k,j]). For R⁺, initialize with the matrix of R itself. Setting every diagonal entry to 1 initially instead computes the version allowing zero-length chains. Vertices on cycles acquire loops in R⁺ via positive-length closed walks; isolated vertices do not.
notation: R⁺ means positive-length reachability; R* also allows length zero.
For finite A, finitely many rounds of intermediate-vertex updates find every reachable pair.
relation_closure__transitive_closure.example: The transitive closure of 1→2→3 adds 1→3 but no loops. For 1→2→1, it adds 1→1 and 2→2.
common_mistakes: Stopping after adding R² once and missing longer chains.
Failing to distinguish whether the initial matrix contains all diagonal pairs.

function_mapping.title: Functions and mappings
function_mapping.summary: A function assigns exactly one value to every domain element; its range need not equal its codomain.
function_mapping.definition: A function f:A→B is a binary relation such that every a∈A corresponds to a unique b∈B. A is the domain, B the codomain, and f(A)={f(a)｜a∈A} the image or range. Both existence of a value for each input and uniqueness for the same input are required.
function_mapping.explanation: For S⊆A, f(S)={f(x)｜x∈S}; for T⊆B, f⁻¹[T]={x∈A｜f(x)∈T}. Preimages exist for every function and do not require invertibility. For finite sets |A|=m, |B|=n with n>0, there are n^m functions. From an empty domain to any codomain there is exactly one empty function; from a nonempty domain to an empty codomain there is none.
notation: f:A→B; f(A)⊆B.
f⁻¹[T] denotes the preimage of T, not automatically an inverse function.
The graph is {(a,f(a))｜a∈A}.
function_mapping.example: Let A={1,2,3}, B={a,b,c}, f(1)=a, f(2)=a, f(3)=b. This is a function with image {a,b}, codomain {a,b,c}, and f⁻¹[{a}]={1,2}.
common_mistakes: Requiring different inputs to have different outputs for a general function.
Thinking an unused codomain element makes the function undefined.
Treating preimage notation as proof of bijectivity.

function_mapping__domain_codomain.title: Domain, codomain, and range
function_mapping__domain_codomain.summary: These sets specify available inputs, the declared target set, and outputs actually attained.
function_mapping__domain_codomain.definition: For f:A→B, the domain is A, the codomain is B, and the range is f(A)={f(x)｜x∈A}. The range is always contained in the codomain but need not equal it.
function_mapping__domain_codomain.explanation: Every domain element must have a unique value. The declared codomain must contain every output, but may have unused elements. Surjectivity depends on the codomain, not just an algebraic expression.
notation: f(A)⊆B; f is surjective ⇔ f(A)=B.
A smaller codomain must still contain every actual output.
function_mapping__domain_codomain.example: The rule n↦2n is not surjective as Z→Z, but is surjective as Z→2Z.
common_mistakes: Always identifying range with codomain.
Enlarging the domain without assigning values to new inputs.

function_mapping__function_counting.title: Counting finite functions and constrained assignments
function_mapping__function_counting.summary: Count functions by choosing one output for each input.
function_mapping__function_counting.definition: For finite |A|=m, |B|=n>0, there are n^m functions A→B. Once some input values are fixed, choose values only for remaining free inputs. Equality or inequality conditions on values need separate treatment.
function_mapping__function_counting.explanation: An empty domain has a unique empty function to any codomain, including the empty set. A nonempty domain has no function to an empty codomain. Function counting differs from relation counting: each row must choose exactly one output, rather than an arbitrary subset.
notation: Each of m labeled inputs has n independent choices; apply the product rule.
A function graph has |A| ordered pairs, but its image may be smaller.
function_mapping__function_counting.example: There are 8 functions from {a,b,c} to {0,1}. If f(a)=0 is fixed, only f(b),f(c) are free, giving 4 functions.
common_mistakes: Counting functions as 2^(mn).
Mechanically using the potentially ambiguous 0^0 without explaining empty-set cases.

function_mapping__image.title: Images of functions
function_mapping__image.summary: An image collects the outputs actually attained by a set of inputs.
function_mapping__image.definition: For f:A→B and S⊆A, the image of S is f(S)={f(x)｜x∈S}. The image f(A) is the range, with f(A)⊆B.
function_mapping__image.explanation: An output produced by several inputs still occurs only once in the image set. Images preserve unions, but generally only f(S∩T)⊆f(S)∩f(T) holds. The reverse inclusion needs an extra condition such as injectivity.
notation: f(S∪T)=f(S)∪f(T).
function_mapping__image.example: For the constant function f:{1,2}→{a}, f({1})∩f({2})={a}, while f({1}∩{2})=∅.
common_mistakes: Assuming an image always has the same size as its input subset.
Interchanging images and intersections without conditions.

function_mapping__preimage.title: Preimages of functions
function_mapping__preimage.summary: A preimage selects all inputs satisfying a specified output condition.
function_mapping__preimage.definition: For f:A→B and T⊆B, f⁻¹[T]={x∈A｜f(x)∈T}. This is a set operation and does not require an inverse function.
function_mapping__preimage.explanation: Preimages preserve unions, intersections, and relative complements. An unused codomain element may have empty preimage. Every preimage element belongs to the domain, and one target value may have several preimage elements.
notation: f⁻¹[T∩U]=f⁻¹[T]∩f⁻¹[U].
f(f⁻¹[T])=T∩f(A).
common_mistakes: Treating preimage notation as an assertion that an inverse function exists.
Choosing one input instead of collecting the entire preimage.

function_mapping__total_single_valued.title: Totality, single-valuedness, and function graphs
function_mapping__total_single_valued.summary: A function graph must give exactly one output for every domain element.
function_mapping__total_single_valued.definition: The graph of f:A→B is a relation in A×B such that for every a∈A there exists a unique b∈B with (a,b) in the graph. Existence is totality, and uniqueness is single-valuedness.
function_mapping__total_single_valued.explanation: Two different inputs may share a value without violating the function definition. Unused codomain elements also cause no problem. The same ordered pairs may cease to be total after changing the domain, so specify both the rule and the sets.
notation: If A=∅, the unique empty relation meets the function conditions for every B.
function_mapping__total_single_valued.example: {(a,0),(b,0)} is a function graph from {a,b} to {0,1}. Enlarging the domain to {a,b,c} without giving c a value makes it cease to be a function graph.
common_mistakes: Confusing injectivity with single-valuedness.
Checking uniqueness only for inputs that appear and missing omitted domain elements.

function_injection.title: Injections, surjections, and bijections
function_injection.summary: Injectivity distinguishes inputs, surjectivity covers the codomain, and bijectivity requires both.
function_injection.definition: f:A→B is injective if f(x)=f(y) implies x=y; it is surjective if every b∈B has some a∈A with f(a)=b. A function satisfying both is bijective. Surjectivity depends on the specified codomain.
function_injection.explanation: For finite A,B, an injection A→B requires |A|≤|B|; a surjection to nonempty B requires |A|≥|B|. When |A|=|B|, a function is injective if and only if it is surjective. This equivalence does not extend directly to infinite sets: n↦n+1 on nonnegative integers is injective but not surjective. Finite bijections are counted by the corresponding permutations.
notation: Injective: different inputs have different outputs.
Surjective: f(A)=B.
A bijection gives a one-to-one correspondence between two sets.
function_injection.example: f:Z→Z, f(n)=2n, is injective but not surjective. Changing the codomain to the even integers 2Z makes the same rule bijective.
common_mistakes: Checking only the absence of output collisions and concluding surjectivity.
Ignoring the effect of changing the codomain on surjectivity.
Applying the finite equal-cardinality equivalence of injectivity and surjectivity to infinite sets.

function_injection__bijection.title: Bijections, finite equal cardinality, and permutations
function_injection__bijection.summary: A bijection gives each output exactly one source and covers every output.
function_injection__bijection.definition: f:A→B is bijective if and only if it is both injective and surjective. For two finite n-element sets, a function is injective if and only if surjective, and there are n! bijections between the sets.
function_injection__bijection.explanation: Equal cardinality of finite sets means a bijection can be constructed; it does not make every given function bijective. Injectivity and surjectivity are no longer equivalent for infinite sets. Constructing a bijection proves equal cardinality and supplies the condition for an inverse function.
notation: For n=0, the unique empty function is also bijective, and 0!=1.
In a bijection every codomain element has exactly one preimage element.
function_injection__bijection.example: There are 3×2×1=6 bijections from {1,2,3} to {a,b,c}; each output may be used only once.
common_mistakes: Inferring every function is bijective from equal set sizes.
Extending the finite injective-surjective equivalence to all infinite sets.

function_injection__injection.title: Injectivity and distinguishing inputs
function_injection__injection.summary: Injectivity requires equal outputs to come only from equal inputs.
function_injection__injection.definition: f:A→B is injective if for all x,y∈A, f(x)=f(y) implies x=y; equivalently, x≠y implies f(x)≠f(y).
function_injection__injection.explanation: An injectivity proof often starts with equal outputs and derives equal inputs. To disprove it, find two distinct inputs with the same value. Restricting an injection to any domain subset preserves injectivity. For finite sets, |A|>|B| rules out an injection.
notation: Every output has at most one preimage element.
Injectivity does not ensure that every codomain element is attained.
function_injection__injection.example: f:Z→Z, f(n)=2n+1, is injective because 2m+1=2n+1 implies m=n.
common_mistakes: Checking a few inputs and claiming injectivity on an infinite domain.
Replacing at most one preimage by at least one preimage.

function_injection__surjection.title: Surjectivity and covering the codomain
function_injection__surjection.summary: Surjectivity requires every codomain object to be reachable from some input.
function_injection__surjection.definition: f:A→B is surjective if for every b∈B there exists a∈A with f(a)=b, that is, f(A)=B.
function_injection__surjection.explanation: To prove surjectivity, take an arbitrary codomain element and construct or prove the existence of an input mapping to it. To disprove it, one unattained codomain element suffices. Changing the codomain while keeping the rule can change surjectivity. For finite nonempty sets, |A|<|B| rules it out.
notation: Every codomain element has at least one preimage element.
Surjectivity allows multiple distinct inputs with the same output.
function_injection__surjection.example: Mapping an integer to its remainder on division by 3 gives a surjection Z→{0,1,2}; every remainder has infinitely many input sources.
common_mistakes: Listing some attainable outputs without handling the rest of the codomain.
Giving a proposed preimage that lies outside the specified domain.

function_composition.title: Function composition
function_composition.summary: Composition feeds one function's output to another; both types and execution order matter.
function_composition.definition: For f:A→B and g:B→C, the composite g∘f:A→C is defined by (g∘f)(a)=g(f(a)): first f, then g. If h:C→D, then h∘(g∘f)=(h∘g)∘f.
function_composition.explanation: Associativity follows from pointwise evaluation and does not allow changing the order. Even for self-maps of one set, g∘f may differ from f∘g. The identity id_A leaves inputs unchanged, with id_B∘f=f and f∘id_A=f. Before composing, check that each stage's image lies in the next stage's domain.
notation: (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)): right to left.
id_A(x)=x.
The composite has f's domain and, as specified, g's codomain.
function_composition.example: On integers, f(n)=n+2 and g(n)=3n give (g∘f)(n)=3n+6, while (f∘g)(n)=3n+2, so they differ.
common_mistakes: Computing g∘f as f(g(x)).
Ignoring types and writing an undefined composition.
Confusing associativity with commutativity.

function_composition__associativity.title: Associativity of function composition
function_composition__associativity.summary: Composition may be regrouped without changing the execution order.
function_composition__associativity.definition: For f:A→B, g:B→C, h:C→D, (h∘g)∘f=h∘(g∘f), both of type A→D.
function_composition__associativity.explanation: On either side, any input a passes through f,g,h to give h(g(f(a))). Associativity allows parentheses to be omitted in long compositions, but neither permits swapping functions nor removes type requirements.
notation: (h∘g)∘f=h∘g∘f=h∘(g∘f).
To prove functions equal, first check their common type, then compare pointwise.
function_composition__associativity.example: The two parenthesizations of employee→department→manager→employee ID give the same final ID.
common_mistakes: Confusing regrouping with reordering.
Checking one input to prove associativity for arbitrary functions.

function_composition__identity.title: Identity functions as composition units
function_composition__identity.summary: An identity function preserves every input and is a composition unit with the correct type.
function_composition__identity.definition: id_A:A→A is defined by id_A(a)=a. For f:A→B, f∘id_A=f and id_B∘f=f.
function_composition__identity.explanation: The subscripts of the left and right units are determined by output and input types and cannot be exchanged freely. An identity function differs from a constant function: on a set with at least two elements, it has different outputs.
notation: f∘id_A=f=id_B∘f.
id_A∘id_A=id_A.
function_composition__identity.example: For f:{1,2}→{a,b}, the input-side identity is on {1,2}, and the output-side identity is on {a,b}.
common_mistakes: Writing the identity as the constant function 1.
Writing id without attending to the sets required by composition.

function_composition__iteration.title: Function iteration and periods
function_composition__iteration.summary: Repeated application of a self-map forms its iterated powers.
function_composition__iteration.definition: For f:A→A, f⁰=id_A and f^(k+1)=f∘f^k. If a positive integer k satisfies f^k=id_A, the least such k is the order of the permutation.
function_composition__iteration.explanation: Iteration is not raising the value f(x) to a power. For a cyclic shift f(x)=x+c mod n, f^k(x)=x+kc mod n. The whole function is the identity only when the equality holds for every input.
notation: f^m∘f^n=f^(m+n), m,n≥0.
f²(x)=f(f(x)), generally not f(x)².
function_composition__iteration.example: Adding 2 on Z₆ becomes the identity after three applications, but not after one or two.
common_mistakes: Writing f² as the square of a function value.
Using one fixed point to decide whether the whole function is the identity.

function_composition__noncommutativity.title: Noncommutativity and special commuting pairs
function_composition__noncommutativity.summary: Composition is generally noncommutative, although particular functions may commute.
function_composition__noncommutativity.definition: Self-maps f,g of the same set commute if f∘g=g∘f. Composition is not generally commutative; for different types the reversed composition may not even be defined.
function_composition__noncommutativity.explanation: One input with different results disproves commutativity for a pair. Proving a pair commutes requires comparison for every input. Transformations acting on independent positions may commute, but this is not a law for all functions.
notation: A single counterexample input proves f∘g≠g∘f.
f∘g=g∘f requires pointwise agreement.
function_composition__noncommutativity.example: On Z, f(n)=n+2, g(n)=3n give the two composites 3n+2 and 3n+6.
common_mistakes: Treating one commuting pair as a general commutative law.
Concluding two functions are equal because they agree on one input.

function_composition__typed_composition.title: Types and execution order in composition
function_composition__typed_composition.summary: Each later stage must accept every output of the preceding stage.
function_composition__typed_composition.definition: For f:A→B, g:B→C, g∘f:A→C is x↦g(f(x)), executing f first. If the specified types do not connect directly, check whether f's actual outputs lie in g's domain and state any restriction of the original domain.
function_composition__typed_composition.explanation: An algebraic expression g(f(x)) need not be defined for every input in the original domain. In finite function tables and data workflows, tracking each intermediate output checks both order and type.
notation: The input of g∘f comes from f's domain; its output lies in g's codomain.
g∘f and f∘g may have different valid types.
function_composition__typed_composition.example: Let f:Z→Z, f(n)=n². If g is defined only on positive integers, g(f(0)) is undefined, so this does not give a composite on all of Z.
common_mistakes: Ignoring whether an intermediate value lies in the next function's domain.
Executing composition symbols from left to right.

function_inverse.title: Inverse functions
function_inverse.summary: A usual two-sided inverse exists exactly for bijections and uniquely recovers inputs from outputs.
function_inverse.definition: An inverse of f:A→B is a function g:B→A such that g∘f=id_A and f∘g=id_B. Such g exists if and only if f is bijective, and is then unique, denoted f⁻¹. This differs from the preimage f⁻¹[T], defined for every function.
function_inverse.explanation: Injectivity gives a unique source for every attained output; surjectivity gives a source for every codomain element. Together they define an inverse on all of B. Restricting the codomain to f(A) makes any injection invertible on that codomain. Inverses reverse the order of two bijections: (g∘f)⁻¹=f⁻¹∘g⁻¹.
notation: f⁻¹:B→A; f⁻¹(f(a))=a and f(f⁻¹(b))=b.
f⁻¹ is usually not the numerical reciprocal 1/f.
f⁻¹[T] is a preimage set and makes sense even without an inverse function.
function_inverse.example: f:Z→2Z, f(n)=2n, is bijective with inverse f⁻¹(m)=m/2, where m must be even. With codomain Z, the same rule is not surjective and has no inverse on all of Z.
common_mistakes: Checking only g∘f=id_A and claiming a two-sided inverse without the other direction.
Writing the inverse as the reciprocal of the output value.
Omitting the inverse's new domain and codomain or confusing preimages with inverse functions.

function_inverse__inverse_composition.title: Reversing order when inverting composite bijections
function_inverse__inverse_composition.summary: To undo a multistep process, undo its last step first.
function_inverse__inverse_composition.definition: If f:A→B and g:B→C are bijections, then (g∘f)⁻¹=f⁻¹∘g⁻¹, a function from C to A.
function_inverse__inverse_composition.explanation: Using associativity, check both composites are identities: f⁻¹∘g⁻¹∘g∘f=id_A and g∘f∘f⁻¹∘g⁻¹=id_C. For more than two bijections, apply their inverses step by step in reverse order.
notation: Original process: first f, then g. Inverse process: first g⁻¹, then f⁻¹.
The types in sequence are C→B→A.
function_inverse__inverse_composition.example: On Z₇, adding 2 then multiplying by 3 gives x↦3x+6. Undo it by multiplying by 5, the inverse of 3 modulo 7, then subtracting 2: y↦5y+5.
common_mistakes: Replacing each step by its inverse without reversing the order.
Using ordinary real division instead of a multiplicative inverse in a finite modular system.

function_inverse__inverse_existence.title: Existence, uniqueness, and codomain of an inverse
function_inverse__inverse_existence.summary: A two-sided inverse exists exactly when the original map is bijective.
function_inverse__inverse_existence.definition: An inverse g:B→A of f:A→B satisfies g∘f=id_A and f∘g=id_B. It exists if and only if f is bijective and is then unique.
function_inverse__inverse_existence.explanation: Injectivity ensures uniqueness of sources and surjectivity ensures a source for every codomain output; together they define an inverse on all of B. For an injection alone, restrict the codomain to f(A) to obtain an inverse. The preimage set f⁻¹[T] makes sense for every function.
notation: The domain of f⁻¹ is B, not A.
f⁻¹ is not the numerical reciprocal 1/f.
function_inverse__inverse_existence.example: n↦2n from Z to Z is not bijective. As a map from Z to 2Z, its inverse is m↦m/2.
common_mistakes: Omitting the inverse's new domain and codomain.
Inferring existence of an inverse because a preimage set is defined.

function_inverse__involution.title: Self-inverse functions (involutions)
function_inverse__involution.summary: A self-inverse function restores the input after two applications.
function_inverse__involution.definition: A self-map f:A→A with f∘f=id_A is an involution or self-inverse function. It is automatically bijective and f⁻¹=f.
function_inverse__involution.explanation: An involution may have fixed points and may swap disjoint pairs of elements. Restoring only some inputs after two applications is insufficient: the identity equation must hold for every input. The identity function itself meets the definition.
notation: f²=id_A ⇒ f⁻¹=f.
The permutation cycles of a finite involution have length 1 or 2 only.
function_inverse__involution.example: On Z₈, f(x)=3x+2 mod 8 satisfies f(f(x))=x, so it is its own inverse.
common_mistakes: Thinking self-inverse means every element is fixed.
Confusing an inverse function with a numerical reciprocal.

function_inverse__left_inverse.title: Left inverses
function_inverse__left_inverse.summary: A left inverse is applied after the original function and recovers each original input.
function_inverse__left_inverse.definition: For f:A→B, a function l:B→A satisfying l∘f=id_A is a left inverse of f.
function_inverse__left_inverse.explanation: A left inverse forces f to be injective: applying l to equal outputs restores equal inputs. It does not ensure surjectivity or f∘l=id_B. For finite sets with nonempty A, an injection has a left inverse by assigning an arbitrary A-element to unused outputs. Empty-set cases require care.
notation: l∘f=id_A.
If A=∅ and B≠∅, the empty function A→B is injective but has no left inverse B→A.
function_inverse__left_inverse.example: For f:N₀→N₀, f(n)=n+1, take l(0)=0 and l(n)=n−1 for n≥1. Then l∘f=id, but f∘l does not restore 0.
common_mistakes: Writing a left inverse condition as f∘l=id.
Claiming every injection with empty domain has a left inverse.

function_inverse__right_inverse.title: Right inverses
function_inverse__right_inverse.summary: A right inverse selects an original input for each target value.
function_inverse__right_inverse.definition: For f:A→B, a function r:B→A satisfying f∘r=id_B is a right inverse of f.
function_inverse__right_inverse.explanation: A right inverse forces f to be surjective, since b=f(r(b)) supplies a preimage for every codomain element. It does not ensure injectivity or r∘f=id_A. For finite sets, choose a preimage for each output of a surjection. Simultaneous choices for arbitrary infinite families involve a choice principle; no unconditional assertion is made here.
notation: f∘r=id_B.
r maps B back to A, but need not restore every A-element.
function_inverse__right_inverse.example: For h:Z→N₀, h(n)=|n|, r(k)=k is a right inverse, but r(h(−1))=1≠−1.
common_mistakes: Equating a right inverse with a two-sided inverse.
Assuming a right inverse is unique when outputs have multiple preimages.

number_prime.title: Divisibility and primes
number_prime.summary: Divisibility describes integer multiples; a prime is an integer greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors.
number_prime.definition: For integers a,b, a divides b, written a∣b, if b=ak for some integer k. A prime p is greater than 1 and has only 1 and p as positive divisors. A nonprime integer greater than 1 is composite. Every integer greater than 1 factors uniquely into prime powers, apart from factor order.
number_prime.explanation: The quotient in divisibility must be an integer: 4∣20, but 4 does not divide 22. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. To test primality of n, check prime factors no greater than √n: if n is composite, at least one member of a nontrivial factor pair is at most √n.
notation: a∣b means b=ak for some k∈ℤ.
n=p₁^α₁⋯pᵣ^αᵣ, where the pᵢ are distinct primes and αᵢ are positive integers.
number_prime.example: 756=2²·3³·7, so it has (2+1)(3+1)(1+1)=24 positive divisors. Each divisor independently chooses an exponent for each prime.
common_mistakes: Counting 1 as prime, undermining the standard uniqueness statement.
Reading a∣b as b∣a.
Checking just one or two integers below n and concluding primality.

number_prime__divisibility.title: Integer divisibility and linear combinations
number_prime__divisibility.summary: A common divisor also divides every corresponding integer linear combination.
number_prime__divisibility.definition: For integers a,b, a∣b means b=ak for some k∈ℤ. If a∣b and a∣c, then a∣(ub+vc) for arbitrary integers u,v. Divisibility is also transitive.
number_prime__divisibility.explanation: Establish divisibility using an integer-multiple representation, not merely the existence of a real quotient. Linear combinations are useful for proving divisibility of expressions and studying gcds.
notation: a∣b ⇔ b=ak, k∈ℤ.
a∣b and a∣c ⇒ a∣(ub+vc).
number_prime__divisibility.example: Since 5∣20 and 5∣35, 5∣(3·20−2·35)=−10; the quotient −2 is still an integer.
common_mistakes: Requiring the quotient to be positive.
Reversing the direction of a∣b.

number_prime__divisor_counting.title: Counting positive and square divisors
number_prime__divisor_counting.summary: Independent choices of prime exponents count different kinds of divisors exactly.
number_prime__divisor_counting.definition: If n=∏pᵢ^αᵢ, each positive divisor is uniquely ∏pᵢ^βᵢ with 0≤βᵢ≤αᵢ. Thus there are ∏(αᵢ+1) positive divisors. A perfect-square divisor requires every βᵢ to be even.
number_prime__divisor_counting.explanation: This is the product rule: every exponent choice corresponds to exactly one divisor. The number of square divisors is ∏(⌊αᵢ/2⌋+1), not simply half the total number of divisors.
notation: The number of square divisors is ∏(⌊αᵢ/2⌋+1).
number_prime__divisor_counting.example: 756=2²·3³·7 has 24 positive divisors; its square divisors are 1,4,9,36.
common_mistakes: Forgetting exponent 0 is a choice.
Allowing odd exponents when counting square divisors.

number_prime__factorization.title: Unique prime factorization
number_prime__factorization.summary: Every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime-power factorization.
number_prime__factorization.definition: Every integer n>1 is a finite product of primes. Combining equal prime factors gives n=p₁^α₁⋯pᵣ^αᵣ with distinct pᵢ and positive integer αᵢ. The factorization is unique apart from factor order.
number_prime__factorization.explanation: Existence follows by repeatedly splitting composites into smaller factors. Uniqueness relies on a prime dividing a product only if it divides a factor. Unique factorization turns divisibility into comparisons of exponents for each prime.
notation: n=∏pᵢ^αᵢ.
Primes are distinct and exponents are positive integers.
number_prime__factorization.example: Factor 756 as 4·189, then 2²·3³·7. Every complete prime factorization must give the same three primes and exponents.
common_mistakes: Leaving a composite factor and claiming the prime factorization is complete.
Including 1 among prime factors and losing the standard uniqueness form.

number_prime__primality.title: Primality and trial division up to the square root
number_prime__primality.summary: A prime has only 1 and itself as positive divisors; trial division need only reach the square root.
number_prime__primality.definition: An integer p>1 is prime if its only positive divisors are 1 and p. A nonprime integer greater than 1 is composite. Every composite n has a prime factor no greater than √n.
number_prime__primality.explanation: If n=ab with 1<a≤b, then a²≤n and a≤√n. Factoring a gives a prime factor no greater than √n. Thus trial division by all primes at most √n suffices: if all fail, n is prime.
notation: 1 is neither prime nor composite.
Test primes p satisfying p≤√n.
number_prime__primality.example: For 53, test only 2,3,5,7. In contrast, 221 is divisible by 13: 221=13·17, so it is composite.
common_mistakes: Omitting equality and misclassifying a square as prime.
Thinking a few small-prime checks suffice for arbitrarily large integers.

number_gcd.title: Greatest common divisors and the Euclidean algorithm
number_gcd.summary: The gcd is the greatest positive common divisor; repeated division with remainder computes it.
number_gcd.definition: For integers a,b not both zero, gcd(a,b) is the greatest positive integer dividing both. If a=bq+r, then gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r). Repeated division gives the gcd as the last nonzero remainder; it can also be expressed as an integer linear combination of a,b.
number_gcd.explanation: The algorithm is correct because (a,b) and (b,a−bq) have exactly the same common divisors. For positive inputs, nonnegative remainders strictly decrease, so it terminates. Substituting the division equations backward gives Bézout coefficients x,y with ax+by=gcd(a,b).
notation: gcd(a,b) is conventionally positive.
ax+by=gcd(a,b) is Bézout's identity.
If gcd(a,b)=1, a and b are coprime.
common_mistakes: Taking the final remainder 0 as the gcd.
Dropping minus signs during backward substitution.
Thinking coprime means both numbers are prime; 8 and 15 are coprime too.

number_gcd__bezout.title: Bézout's identity
number_gcd__bezout.summary: The gcd is an integer linear combination of the original integers.
number_gcd__bezout.definition: For integers a,b not both zero, some integers x,y satisfy ax+by=gcd(a,b). In particular, gcd(a,b)=1 if and only if 1 is an integer linear combination of a,b.
number_gcd__bezout.explanation: Every integer linear combination is divisible by the gcd; Bézout's identity says the gcd itself also occurs. This underlies modular inverses, divisibility cancellation, and Diophantine solvability. The extended Euclidean algorithm finds specific coefficients.
notation: ax+by=gcd(a,b).
If gcd(a,b)=1, then ax+by=1 for some integers x,y.
number_gcd__bezout.example: 35·(−5)+22·8=1, so 35 and 22 are coprime. These coefficients also help find the inverse of 35 modulo 22.
common_mistakes: Restricting Bézout coefficients to nonnegative integers.
Using an incorrect remainder absent from the original division chain in backward substitution.

number_gcd__coprimality.title: Coprimality and divisibility cancellation
number_gcd__coprimality.summary: Coprimality allows a factor to be canceled from a divisibility relation.
number_gcd__coprimality.definition: a,b are coprime if gcd(a,b)=1. If gcd(a,b)=1 and a∣bc, then a∣c. Coprimality does not require a and b individually to be prime.
number_gcd__coprimality.explanation: Multiply au+bv=1 by c to obtain c=auc+bvc. If a∣bc, both terms on the right are divisible by a. This proves the precise cancellation condition.
notation: gcd(a,b)=1.
a∣bc and gcd(a,b)=1 ⇒ a∣c.
number_gcd__coprimality.example: 8 and 15 are coprime, so 8∣15c implies 8∣c. From 8∣2c, however, 2 cannot be canceled in this way.
common_mistakes: Inferring a∣c from a∣bc without checking coprimality.
Equating distinct numbers with coprime numbers.

number_gcd__diophantine.title: Linear Diophantine equations in two variables
number_gcd__diophantine.summary: Integer solvability depends on whether the gcd divides the right-hand side.
number_gcd__diophantine.definition: Let a,b not both be zero and g=gcd(a,b). The equation ax+by=c has integer solutions if and only if g∣c. Given one solution (x₀,y₀), all solutions are x=x₀+(b/g)t, y=y₀−(a/g)t, t∈ℤ.
number_gcd__diophantine.explanation: Necessity follows because g divides each term on the left; sufficiency follows by multiplying Bézout's identity by c/g. The parameterization describes integer points, not arbitrary real solutions.
notation: ax+by=c, x,y∈ℤ.
One integer parameter t describes the solution set.
number_gcd__diophantine.example: A solution of 35x+22y=1 is (−5,8); all solutions are (−5+22t,8−35t).
common_mistakes: Treating real solvability as integer solvability.
Forgetting to divide the parameter step sizes by g.

number_gcd__euclidean.title: Decreasing remainders in the Euclidean algorithm
number_gcd__euclidean.summary: Successive divisions reduce values while preserving the set of common divisors.
number_gcd__euclidean.definition: For a≥b>0, write a=bq+r with 0≤r<b. Then gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r). Iterate until the remainder is zero; the preceding nonzero remainder is the gcd.
number_gcd__euclidean.explanation: Each remainder is strictly smaller than the previous positive divisor, so the positive remainder chain is finite. The final identity gcd(d,0)=d, not 0, explains how to read the result.
notation: a=bq+r, 0≤r<b.
gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r).
common_mistakes: Reading the quotient sequence as the gcd.
Taking 0 rather than the preceding nonzero remainder at termination.

number_gcd__extended_euclidean.title: The extended Euclidean algorithm
number_gcd__extended_euclidean.summary: Tracking linear-combination coefficients alongside remainders computes Bézout coefficients.
number_gcd__extended_euclidean.definition: The extended Euclidean algorithm outputs not just gcd(a,b) but x,y with ax+by=gcd(a,b). Substitute backward from the last nonzero remainder, or maintain each remainder's a,b coefficients during iteration.
number_gcd__extended_euclidean.explanation: Every substitution must use the corresponding division equation. Coefficients may be negative. Substituting the final coefficients directly into the original equation is the simplest independent check.
notation: rᵢ=sᵢa+tᵢb.
The last nonzero remainder yields one pair of required coefficients.
common_mistakes: Replacing a remainder without retaining the whole surrounding parentheses.
Finding coefficients but swapping their corresponding a,b positions.

number_gcd__gcd_definition.title: The gcd and common constraints
number_gcd__gcd_definition.summary: The gcd is the greatest positive unit measuring both integers exactly.
number_gcd__gcd_definition.definition: For a,b not both zero, gcd(a,b) is their greatest positive common divisor. Every common divisor divides gcd(a,b), which itself divides a and b. In prime factorizations, the gcd takes the smaller exponent for each common prime.
number_gcd__gcd_definition.explanation: In geometric subdivision, allowable integer sizes often must divide both lengths, making the gcd the maximum allowable size. gcd(0,b)=|b| when b≠0.
notation: g=gcd(a,b)>0.
d∣a and d∣b ⇒ d∣g.
number_gcd__gcd_definition.example: An 84 cm by 30 cm rectangle tiled along its sides by equal squares of integer side length has maximum square side gcd(84,30)=6 cm.
common_mistakes: Confusing the gcd with the lcm.
Ignoring the convention that the gcd is positive.

number_congruence.title: Congruence and modular arithmetic
number_congruence.summary: Congruence groups integers differing by a multiple of the modulus and supports addition, subtraction, multiplication, and nonnegative powers.
number_congruence.definition: For integers a,b and a positive integer m, a≡b(mod m) means m∣(a−b). Every integer has a unique least nonnegative remainder r modulo m with 0≤r<m. Congruence is an equivalence relation on the integers.
number_congruence.explanation: Values may be reduced before addition or multiplication. For example, −17≡3(mod 5); a negative number is not the least nonnegative remainder. Cancellation needs a condition: ca≡cb(mod m) does not generally permit canceling c with the same modulus; gcd(c,m)=1 allows this.
notation: a≡b(mod m) means a−b=km for some k∈ℤ.
[a]ₘ denotes the congruence class of a modulo m.
number_congruence.example: 2·1≡2·5(mod 8), but 1 and 5 are not congruent modulo 8. The common factor 2 is not coprime to 8 and cannot simply be canceled.
common_mistakes: Confusing equal remainders with equal integers.
Canceling arbitrary nonunits without changing the modulus.
Failing to adjust a negative integer's remainder to 0 through m−1.

number_congruence__arithmetic.title: Congruence arithmetic and periods of modular powers
number_congruence__arithmetic.summary: Reduce intermediate remainders to avoid unnecessarily large integers.
number_congruence__arithmetic.definition: If a≡b(mod m) and c≡d(mod m), then a±c≡b±d and ac≡bd(mod m). For nonnegative k, aᵏ≡bᵏ(mod m). Repeated multiplication may yield useful remainder cycles.
number_congruence__arithmetic.explanation: Compatibility with addition, subtraction, and multiplication follows because the relevant differences are divisible by m. For large powers, compute a short initial cycle or use repeated squaring. Ordinary real division does not always preserve congruence.
notation: Compute (a+b) mod m from the separate remainders.
Compute aᵏ mod m by reducing after each multiplication.
number_congruence__arithmetic.example: Modulo 10, 7,7²,7³,7⁴ have remainders 7,9,3,1, so powers of 7 repeat every 4 steps.
common_mistakes: Directly reducing the exponent modulo m.
Assuming a cycle from a few repeated terms without justifying its continuation.

number_congruence__cancellation.title: Coprimality in congruence cancellation
number_congruence__cancellation.summary: Canceling a common factor may require changing the modulus.
number_congruence__cancellation.definition: Let m>0 and g=gcd(c,m). Then ca≡cb(mod m) is equivalent to a≡b(mod m/g). In particular, if g=1, c may be canceled while keeping modulus m.
number_congruence__cancellation.explanation: From m∣c(a−b), dividing out g leaves coprime m/g and c/g, so m/g divides a−b. Keeping the old modulus when the factors are not coprime generally loses solutions.
notation: ca≡cb(mod m) ⇔ a≡b(mod m/gcd(c,m)).
If gcd(c,m)=1, c is invertible.
number_congruence__cancellation.example: 2x≡2(mod8) is equivalent to x≡1(mod4), giving two remainder solutions modulo 8: 1,5.
common_mistakes: Always canceling c with the original modulus.
Canceling coefficients and the modulus without checking their gcd.

number_congruence__modular_exponentiatio.title: Modular power periods and repeated squaring
number_congruence__modular_exponentiatio.summary: Periods and the binary expansion of an exponent make modular exponentiation efficient.
number_congruence__modular_exponentiatio.definition: To compute aᵏ mod m, repeatedly square to obtain the remainders of a,a²,a⁴,a⁸,…, then multiply according to the binary expansion of k. If aᵗ≡1(mod m) is established, nonnegative exponents may be reduced modulo the period t.
number_congruence__modular_exponentiatio.explanation: Reducing after every multiplication preserves the final remainder. Do not simply reduce the exponent modulo m or assume an unproved period from a few apparently repeated terms.
notation: k=Σbᵢ2ⁱ, bᵢ∈{0,1}.
aᵏ≡∏(a^(2ⁱ))^bᵢ(mod m).
number_congruence__modular_exponentiatio.example: Powers of 7 have period 4 modulo 10, so 7¹⁰³≡7³. Repeated squaring gives the same result.
common_mistakes: Taking the modulus m itself as the exponent period.
Writing a^(u+v) incorrectly as aᵘ+aᵛ.

number_congruence__residue_classes.title: Congruence as an equivalence relation and residue classes
number_congruence__residue_classes.summary: Congruence partitions all integers into finitely many residue classes.
number_congruence__residue_classes.definition: For m>0, a≡b(mod m) if and only if m∣(a−b). Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity hold, partitioning ℤ into m residue classes represented by 0 through m−1.
number_congruence__residue_classes.explanation: Different representatives can describe the same class: −17,3,8 are in one class modulo 5, although they are not equal as integers. The least nonnegative remainder is just a standard representative.
notation: [a]ₘ={a+km:k∈ℤ}.
Standard representatives satisfy 0≤r<m.
number_congruence__residue_classes.example: −17=(−4)·5+3, so [−17]₅=[3]₅ and the standard representative is 3.
common_mistakes: Confusing equal residue classes with equal integers.
Calling a negative representative the least nonnegative remainder.

number_linear_congruence.title: Linear congruences
number_linear_congruence.summary: Solvability of ax≡b(mod m) is determined by whether gcd(a,m) divides b.
number_linear_congruence.definition: Let m be positive and a,b integers, and set g=gcd(a,m). The congruence ax≡b(mod m) has an integer solution if and only if g∣b. If solvable, it has exactly g distinct remainder solutions modulo m. Dividing a,b,m by g gives a coefficient coprime to the new modulus.
number_linear_congruence.explanation: The congruence is equivalent to ax−my=b. When solvable, use the extended Euclidean algorithm to invert the reduced coefficient, find a solution modulo m/g, and lift it to g solutions modulo m. The modulus must be divided too; canceling only the coefficients is invalid.
notation: g=gcd(a,m).
If x₀ solves the reduced congruence modulo m/g, the original solutions modulo m are x₀+k(m/g), k=0,…,g−1.
number_linear_congruence.example: 6x≡8(mod14) reduces, by dividing the coefficient, right-hand side, and modulus by 2, to 3x≡4(mod7). The inverse of 3 modulo 7 is 5, so x≡6(mod7), yielding 6 and 13 modulo 14.
common_mistakes: Seeking an inverse before checking g∣b.
Replacing the reduced modulus m/g by the original m.
Giving one solution and missing the other g−1.

number_linear_congruence__inverses.title: Modular inverses and coprime linear congruences
number_linear_congruence__inverses.summary: A coefficient coprime to the modulus has an inverse giving a unique residue-class solution.
number_linear_congruence__inverses.definition: A multiplicative inverse of a modulo m is an integer u satisfying au≡1(mod m). It exists if and only if gcd(a,m)=1, and is unique modulo m. Then ax≡b(mod m) has solution x≡ub(mod m).
number_linear_congruence__inverses.explanation: The extended Euclidean algorithm gives au+mv=1, so u is an inverse. This is not the real reciprocal 1/a, and an inverse cannot be forced when the coefficient and modulus are not coprime.
notation: au≡1(mod m).
gcd(a,m)=1 ⇒ x≡a⁻¹b(mod m).
number_linear_congruence__inverses.example: 7·15=105≡1(mod26), so the inverse of 7 modulo 26 is 15.
common_mistakes: Treating the fraction 1/a as an integer modular inverse.
Using an inverse for modulus m with a different modulus.

number_linear_congruence__lifting.title: Reducing congruences and lifting all remainder solutions
number_linear_congruence__lifting.summary: For solvable noncoprime coefficients, reduction must be followed by listing all solutions for the original modulus.
number_linear_congruence__lifting.definition: If g=gcd(a,m) and g∣b, then ax≡b(mod m) is equivalent to (a/g)x≡b/g(mod m/g). After finding a reduced solution x₀, the solutions modulo m are x₀+k(m/g), k=0,…,g−1.
