number_linear_congruence__lifting.explanation: Dividing the divisibility relation by g changes the modulus as well. The resulting g solutions are pairwise distinct modulo the original modulus. Keeping only x₀ loses other congruence classes.
notation: m′=m/g.
Lift representatives to modulus m as x₀+k m′.
number_linear_congruence__lifting.example: 6x≡8(mod14) reduces to 3x≡4(mod7), giving x≡6(mod7), so the solutions modulo 14 are 6,13.
common_mistakes: Canceling coefficients without changing the modulus.
Presenting the unique reduced solution as unique for the original modulus.

number_linear_congruence__solvability.title: The gcd condition for solvability of linear congruences
number_linear_congruence__solvability.summary: First check whether gcd(a,m) divides b.
number_linear_congruence__solvability.definition: Let m>0 and g=gcd(a,m). The congruence ax≡b(mod m) is solvable if and only if g∣b. Necessity follows from ax−my=b, and sufficiency from a suitable multiple of Bézout's identity.
number_linear_congruence__solvability.explanation: This check needs no explicit solution and often immediately rules out incompatible conditions. When solvable, there are g residue-class solutions modulo m. A noncoprime coefficient therefore does not automatically mean no solution.
notation: g∣b is the solvability condition.
If solvable, there are g residue-class solutions modulo m.
number_linear_congruence__solvability.example: 6x≡5(mod9) has no solution, but 6x≡3(mod9) does, since gcd(6,9)=3 divides only the latter right-hand side.
common_mistakes: Treating g>1 as automatic insolubility.
Checking only whether a divides b and ignoring the modulus m.

number_inverse_crt.title: The Chinese remainder theorem
number_inverse_crt.summary: Congruences with pairwise coprime moduli combine into one residue class modulo their product.
number_inverse_crt.definition: If positive integers m₁,…,mᵣ are pairwise coprime, then any integer residues a₁,…,aᵣ give a solvable system x≡aᵢ(mod mᵢ), unique modulo M=m₁⋯mᵣ. Set Mᵢ=M/mᵢ and choose uᵢ with Mᵢuᵢ≡1(mod mᵢ); then x≡ΣaᵢMᵢuᵢ(mod M).
number_inverse_crt.explanation: The theorem gives both existence and uniqueness. For noncoprime moduli, uniqueness modulo the product cannot be assumed. Two conditions require their residue difference to be divisible by the gcd of the moduli; the solution period is their lcm.
notation: M=∏mᵢ, Mᵢ=M/mᵢ.
Mᵢ has an inverse modulo mᵢ because gcd(Mᵢ,mᵢ)=1.
number_inverse_crt.example: x≡2(mod3), x≡3(mod5) gives x≡8(mod15). The integer 8 meets both conditions. Any two solutions differ by a multiple of both 3 and 5, hence of 15.
common_mistakes: Replacing pairwise coprimality with the collective gcd being 1.
Claiming uniqueness modulo the product for noncoprime moduli.
Finding one integer without stating the full solution period.

number_inverse_crt__compatibility.title: Compatibility and periods for noncoprime moduli
number_inverse_crt__compatibility.summary: Noncoprime congruence conditions can conflict; if solvable, their period is the lcm.
number_inverse_crt__compatibility.definition: For x≡a(mod m), x≡b(mod n), let g=gcd(m,n). The system is solvable if and only if g∣(a−b); if solvable, its solution is unique modulo lcm(m,n).
number_inverse_crt__compatibility.explanation: The conditions must give the same remainder modulo their common factor g to come from one integer. Substitute x=a+mt into the second condition to reduce solvability to a linear congruence.
notation: gcd(m,n)∣(a−b).
lcm(m,n)=mn/gcd(m,n).
number_inverse_crt__compatibility.example: x≡1(mod4), x≡3(mod6) gives x≡9(mod12), rather than a single class modulo 24.
common_mistakes: Writing the period as mn unconditionally.
Declaring all noncoprime systems unsolvable.

number_inverse_crt__construction.title: CRT construction with inverses
number_inverse_crt__construction.summary: Construct weights equal to 1 at their own modulus and 0 at the others, then combine the residues.
number_inverse_crt__construction.definition: Let M=∏mᵢ, Mᵢ=M/mᵢ, and choose uᵢ with Mᵢuᵢ≡1(mod mᵢ). With pairwise coprime moduli, x=ΣaᵢMᵢuᵢ satisfies every congruence.
number_inverse_crt__construction.explanation: Modulo mᵢ, its own weight Mᵢuᵢ is 1, while every other weight contains mᵢ and is 0. Each term therefore independently supplies the desired residue at its modulus. Finally reduce the sum to 0 through M−1.
notation: wᵢ=Mᵢuᵢ.
wᵢ≡1(mod mᵢ), wᵢ≡0(mod mⱼ), j≠i.
number_inverse_crt__construction.example: For moduli 5,7, M=35 and weights 21,15 work. Residues 4,6 give x≡4·21+6·15=174≡34(mod35).
common_mistakes: Computing the inverse of mᵢ modulo Mᵢ instead of Mᵢ modulo mᵢ.
Omitting Mᵢ and adding only residues times inverses.

number_inverse_crt__coprime_systems.title: Combining systems with coprime moduli
number_inverse_crt__coprime_systems.summary: For pairwise coprime moduli, each residue tuple gives a unique class modulo their product.
number_inverse_crt__coprime_systems.definition: For pairwise coprime positive m₁,…,mᵣ, any conditions x≡aᵢ(mod mᵢ) are simultaneously solvable, and all solutions form one class modulo M=∏mᵢ.
number_inverse_crt__coprime_systems.explanation: Combine conditions successively: merge two into one modulo their product, then merge with later conditions. Check every pair of moduli, rather than only the collective gcd.
notation: The full solution period is M=∏mᵢ.
Pairwise coprime means gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)=1 for every i≠j.
common_mistakes: Finding one satisfying integer and ignoring the full period.
Confusing collective gcd 1 with pairwise coprimality.

number_euler_fermat.title: Euler's theorem and Fermat's little theorem
number_euler_fermat.summary: Euler's theorem gives a modular power period for coprime integers; Fermat's little theorem is a prime-modulus special case.
number_euler_fermat.definition: For positive n, Euler's totient φ(n) counts integers from 1 through n coprime to n. If gcd(a,n)=1, then a^φ(n)≡1(mod n). If p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p−1)≡1(mod p). Equivalently, a^p≡a(mod p) for every integer a.
number_euler_fermat.explanation: Check coprimality before reducing a large exponent. If the distinct prime factors of n are p₁,…,pᵣ, then φ(n)=n∏(1−1/pᵢ). The form a^p≡a also holds when p divides a, but dividing by a to get a^(p−1)≡1 requires excluding that case.
notation: φ(p)=p−1 for prime p.
gcd(a,n)=1 ⇒ a^φ(n)≡1(mod n).
common_mistakes: Using Euler's theorem without checking coprimality.
Applying Fermat's little theorem to a composite as if it were prime.
Interpreting φ(n) as the number of prime factors of n.

number_euler_fermat__euler_theorem.title: Euler's theorem and reduced residue systems
number_euler_fermat__euler_theorem.summary: For a base coprime to the modulus, exponents may be reduced using the totient period.
number_euler_fermat__euler_theorem.definition: If n>1 and gcd(a,n)=1, then a^φ(n)≡1(mod n). The residue classes coprime to n form a reduced residue system; multiplication by the unit a permutes them.
number_euler_fermat__euler_theorem.explanation: Multiply all reduced residues in the proof and cancel their invertible product. In applications, check coprimality first, then write the exponent as a multiple of φ(n) plus a remainder.
notation: gcd(a,n)=1 is a hypothesis of Euler's theorem.
a^(kφ(n)+r)≡aʳ(mod n).
common_mistakes: Subtracting multiples of φ(n) from an exponent with a noncoprime base.
Treating cancellation of the reduced-residue product as unconditional division.

number_euler_fermat__fermat_theorem.title: Fermat's little theorem and powers modulo primes
number_euler_fermat__fermat_theorem.summary: For a prime modulus, coprime bases satisfy the exponent p−1 identity.
number_euler_fermat__fermat_theorem.definition: If p is prime and p∤a, then a^(p−1)≡1(mod p). The equivalent universal form is aᵖ≡a(mod p) for every integer a. A single base satisfying the congruence does not conversely prove the modulus prime.
number_euler_fermat__fermat_theorem.explanation: When p∣a, aᵖ≡a still says 0≡0, but a^(p−1)≡1 generally fails. The two forms have different conditions. A composite can satisfy similar congruences for particular bases, so one successful test does not establish primality.
notation: p prime and p∤a ⇒ a^(p−1)≡1(mod p).
p prime ⇒ aᵖ≡a(mod p) for every integer a.
number_euler_fermat__fermat_theorem.example: For 2¹⁰⁰⁰ modulo 13, reduce 1000 modulo 12 to 4, giving 2⁴≡3(mod13).
common_mistakes: Mixing the hypotheses of the two Fermat forms.
Assuming the converse of the theorem.

number_euler_fermat__pseudoprimes.title: Fermat pseudoprimes and limits of the converse
number_euler_fermat__pseudoprimes.summary: A composite can pass a Fermat-type congruence test for a coprime base.
number_euler_fermat__pseudoprimes.definition: For composite n>1 and gcd(a,n)=1, if a^(n−1)≡1(mod n), then n is a Fermat pseudoprime to base a. Fermat's little theorem supplies a necessary property of primes, not a direct converse primality test.
number_euler_fermat__pseudoprimes.explanation: A successful test for one base establishes only that congruence. A nontrivial factor proves compositeness; primality needs other complete justification and cannot be replaced by one test that did not fail.
notation: n is composite and a^(n−1)≡1(mod n).
The base a must be coprime to n.
number_euler_fermat__pseudoprimes.example: 341=11·31, and 2¹⁰=1024≡1(mod341), so 2³⁴⁰≡1. Thus 341 is a base-2 Fermat pseudoprime.
common_mistakes: Treating Fermat's little theorem as an if-and-only-if statement.
Using pseudoprime terminology without verifying compositeness and coprimality.

number_euler_fermat__totient.title: Euler's totient and counting coprime residues
number_euler_fermat__totient.summary: The totient counts invertible elements in a complete residue period.
number_euler_fermat__totient.definition: φ(n) is the number of integers from 1 through n coprime to n. If p₁,…,pᵣ are the distinct prime factors of n, then φ(n)=n∏(1−1/pᵢ); for prime p, φ(p)=p−1.
number_euler_fermat__totient.explanation: Exclude integers divisible by the prime factors of n; inclusion-exclusion gives the product formula. Prime powers are already included in n, so do not repeat the same prime in the product.
notation: φ(pᵏ)=pᵏ−pᵏ⁻¹.
common_mistakes: Excluding repeatedly for each power of the same prime.
Interpreting φ(n) as the number of primes below n.

number_rsa.title: RSA public-key cryptography
number_rsa.summary: RSA uses related exponents for modular powers; the small course parameters are for demonstration only.
number_rsa.definition: Teaching RSA chooses distinct primes p,q, sets n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1), chooses positive e coprime to φ(n), and finds d with ed≡1(mod φ(n)). For 0≤m<n, textbook modular exponentiation gives c≡m^e(mod n) and m≡c^d(mod n).
number_rsa.explanation: Prove correctness separately modulo p and q, then combine by CRT. If a prime divides m, both sides are 0 for that modulus; otherwise apply Fermat's little theorem. Small primes and unpadded textbook RSA here are toy demonstrations, unsuitable for real encryption; real systems also require standard padding, randomness, and secure implementation.
notation: n is the modulus, e the public exponent, and d the corresponding private exponent.
ed≡1(mod φ(n)); the exponent inverse is not taken modulo n.
number_rsa.example: Toy parameters p=5,q=11 give n=55,φ(n)=40. Choose e=3,d=27 since 3·27=81≡1(mod40). The message m=7 encrypts to c=13, and 13²⁷ mod55 restores 7.
common_mistakes: Computing d as the inverse of e modulo n.
Using Euler's theorem alone for messages not coprime to n and omitting cases or CRT.
Treating tiny primes or unpadded examples as secure real encryption.

number_rsa__crt_correctness.title: CRT correctness of RSA for noncoprime messages
number_rsa__crt_correctness.summary: Correctness must cover messages divisible by a prime factor of the modulus.
number_rsa__crt_correctness.definition: Let p,q be distinct primes, n=pq, and e,d positive integers such that ed−1 is a multiple of (p−1)(q−1). For every integer m, m^(ed)≡m(mod p) and m^(ed)≡m(mod q), hence m^(ed)≡m(mod n). For each prime, consider separately whether it divides m, then use CRT.
number_rsa__crt_correctness.explanation: If p∣m, both sides are 0 modulo p; otherwise apply Fermat's little theorem. Treat q similarly, then combine because p,q are coprime. No assumption gcd(m,n)=1 is needed. This proves algebraic correctness of the teaching transformation, not real encryption security.
notation: Consider p∣m and p∤m separately.
Congruence modulo both p and q ⇒ congruence modulo pq.
number_rsa__crt_correctness.example: For toy n=55,e=3,d=27,m=5, the message is not coprime to n, but ciphertext 15 raised to the 27th power is still 5 modulo 55.
common_mistakes: Applying Euler's theorem directly to noncoprime m.
Proving the result only for coprime messages and claiming all messages are covered.

number_rsa__key_generation.title: Generating exponents for teaching RSA
number_rsa__key_generation.summary: The public exponent is coprime to φ(n); its modular inverse gives the private exponent.
number_rsa__key_generation.definition: In an RSA construction for teaching only, choose distinct primes p,q, set n=pq and φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1), choose gcd(e,φ(n))=1, and find a positive representative d satisfying ed≡1(mod φ(n)).
number_rsa__key_generation.explanation: The inverse modulus is φ(n), not n. Once e is chosen, use the extended Euclidean algorithm to find d. These small parameters and unpadded textbook constructions illustrate algebraic relations and are unsuitable for secure real encryption.
notation: d≡e⁻¹(mod φ(n)).
number_rsa__key_generation.example: Toy p=7,q=11 give n=77,φ(n)=60. For e=7, choose d=43 since 7·43=301≡1(mod60).
common_mistakes: Choosing the same prime twice while still using (p−1)(q−1).
Finding d modulo n by mistake.

q_relation_property_02.title: Vacuous truth in the empty relation
q_relation_property_02.statement: On the nonempty set A={x,y}, let R=∅. Which properties hold?
q_relation_property_02.explanation: The empty relation lacks (x,x) and (y,y), so it is not reflexive. The antecedents of symmetry, antisymmetry, and transitivity require ordered pairs in R. Since there are none, no instance violates these implications.
q_relation_property_02.grading_criteria: Select exactly B,C,D. Explain that nonempty A causes reflexivity to fail, while the other three hold because there are no counterexamples.

q_relation_property_03.title: Failure of symmetry does not imply antisymmetry
q_relation_property_03.statement: Someone claims: 'Every relation that is not symmetric must be antisymmetric.' Give a counterexample on A={1,2,3}, and identify explicit witnesses for both failures.
q_relation_property_03.answer_text: Take R={(1,2),(2,1),(2,3)}. Symmetry fails because (2,3) is present but (3,2) is absent. Antisymmetry also fails because 1≠2 and both (1,2),(2,1) belong to R.
q_relation_property_03.explanation: Failure of symmetry needs an edge missing its reverse; failure of antisymmetry needs a bidirectional pair of distinct elements. Both kinds of witness can occur in one relation. The different technical term 'asymmetric relation' is not introduced here.
q_relation_property_03.grading_criteria: Give an explicit relation and separate witnesses for failure of symmetry and antisymmetry; property names alone are insufficient.

q_relation_property_04.title: Is a union of transitive relations transitive?
q_relation_property_04.statement: Must R∪S be transitive when R and S are transitive relations on the same set? Give a proof or a minimal explicit counterexample, and check R and S individually for transitivity.
q_relation_property_04.answer_text: No. On A={1,2,3}, take R={(1,2)}, S={(2,3)}. Each has no composable pair of edges and is transitive. Their union contains (1,2),(2,3) but not (1,3), so it is not transitive.
q_relation_property_04.explanation: The two antecedent edges of transitivity may come from different relations. Separate transitivity does not constrain such mixed two-step chains, so union does not preserve transitivity.
q_relation_property_04.grading_criteria: Verify that both relations in the counterexample are themselves transitive and identify the missing pair (1,3) in their union.

q_relation_equivalence_01.title: Equivalence classes modulo three
q_relation_equivalence_01.statement: On A={0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}, define aRb if and only if 3 divides a−b. List all distinct equivalence classes and find |R|.
q_relation_equivalence_01.explanation: Classes are determined by remainders modulo 3. Each contains 3 elements and contributes all 3² within-class ordered pairs. No pairs join different classes, so |R|=3×9=27.
q_relation_equivalence_01.grading_criteria: List three distinct classes covering A. Count pairs by summing squared class sizes and include diagonal pairs.

q_relation_equivalence_02.title: Recognizing partitions
q_relation_equivalence_02.statement: Let A={1,2,3,4}. Which families are partitions of A?
q_relation_equivalence_02.explanation: In A and C, blocks are nonempty, pairwise disjoint, and cover A. The first two blocks of B overlap at 2. D omits 4 from its union.
q_relation_equivalence_02.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,C and identify B's overlapping element and D's omitted element.

q_relation_equivalence_03.title: Classifying binary strings by weight
q_relation_equivalence_03.statement: Let A be all binary strings of length 4. Two strings are equivalent when they contain the same number of 1s. Find the number of classes, each class size, and the total number of ordered pairs in the equivalence relation.
q_relation_equivalence_03.answer_text: There are 5 classes, indexed by 0,1,2,3,4 ones, with sizes 1,4,6,4,1. The total number of ordered pairs is 70.
q_relation_equivalence_03.explanation: A string with k ones chooses k of four positions, giving C(4,0),C(4,1),C(4,2),C(4,3),C(4,4) strings. Only strings of equal weight are related, so the relation size is 1²+4²+6²+4²+1²=70.
q_relation_equivalence_03.grading_criteria: Give all 5 classes and their sizes, then count ordered pairs within classes; simply adding the 16 strings is insufficient.

q_relation_equivalence_04.title: Relation inclusion and partition refinement
q_relation_equivalence_04.statement: Let R,S be equivalence relations on A. Prove that R⊆S if and only if every R-class is contained in some S-class.
q_relation_equivalence_04.answer_text: If R⊆S, then for every a, x∈[a]_R implies xRa, hence xSa, so [a]_R⊆[a]_S. Conversely, suppose every R-class lies in an S-class. If aRb, then a,b are in the same R-class and thus the same S-class, so aSb. Therefore R⊆S.
q_relation_equivalence_04.explanation: Fewer allowed links generally give a finer partition. The converse must use that all elements of one R-class lie in one S-class, rather than choosing separate classes for each element.
q_relation_equivalence_04.grading_criteria: Prove both directions and explain why containment of an R-class makes any two of its elements S-related. The statement also holds when A is empty.

q_relation_order_01.title: Covers in a divisibility poset
q_relation_order_01.statement: Order A={1,2,3,6,12} by divisibility. List every covering pair (a,b), where b covers a, and give the least and greatest elements.
q_relation_order_01.answer_text: The covering pairs are (1,2),(1,3),(2,6),(3,6),(6,12). The least element is 1 and the greatest is 12.
q_relation_order_01.explanation: For example, 2|12, but 6 is an intermediate element with 2|6|12, so (2,12) is not a cover. The number 1 divides every element, and every element divides 12.
q_relation_order_01.grading_criteria: Remove all comparisons obtainable through intermediate elements when listing covers. State least and greatest relative to the given set and divisibility relation.

q_relation_order_02.title: Bounds in a power-set poset
q_relation_order_02.statement: Let U={a,b,c} and order P(U) by inclusion. For S={{a},{b}}, find all upper bounds, all lower bounds, the least upper bound, and the greatest lower bound.
q_relation_order_02.answer_text: Upper bounds: {a,b}, {a,b,c}. The only lower bound is ∅. The least upper bound is {a,b}; the greatest lower bound is ∅.
q_relation_order_02.explanation: An upper bound must contain both a and b, giving {a,b} or {a,b,c}. A lower bound must lie in both {a} and {b}, so it can only be empty. Union gives the least upper bound and intersection the greatest lower bound.
q_relation_order_02.grading_criteria: Distinguish bounds, which are elements of P(U), from the family S. List all bounds rather than only the two optimal ones.

q_relation_order_03.title: Minimal and maximal need not mean least and greatest
q_relation_order_03.statement: Order A={2,3,6,10} by divisibility. Which statements are correct?
q_relation_order_03.explanation: Both 2 and 3 have no strictly smaller divisor in A and are minimal. Both 6 and 10 have no strictly greater multiple in A and are maximal. Since 3 divides neither 2 nor 10, it is not least. Since 10 does not divide 6, 6 is not greatest. In fact there is neither a least nor a greatest element.
q_relation_order_03.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,C and use incomparable elements to explain why B,D fail.

q_relation_order_04.title: A unique minimal element and finiteness
q_relation_order_04.statement: Prove that a nonempty finite poset with exactly one minimal element m has m as its least element. Then show that the conclusion can fail without finiteness.
q_relation_order_04.answer_text: Take any x. If x is not minimal, choose a strictly smaller element. Finiteness makes this descent terminate at a minimal element, necessarily m, so m≤x. As x was arbitrary, m is least. For an infinite counterexample, take A=Z∪{a}, with the usual order on integers and a comparable only to itself. The integer chain has no minimal element, so a is the unique minimal element. It is incomparable with every integer and is not least.
q_relation_order_04.explanation: A finite poset has no infinite strictly descending chain, so a minimal element lies below every element. In an infinite poset, some branches may descend forever with no minimal element, and the unique existing minimal element need not lie below them.
q_relation_order_04.grading_criteria: Explain why descent terminates and how uniqueness is used. Check that the infinite example is a poset, has exactly one minimal element, and has no least element.

q_relation_closure_01.title: Two closures of a chain relation
q_relation_closure_01.statement: On A={1,2,3}, let R={(1,2),(2,3)}. Find R⁺ and R* and their cardinalities, where R⁺ is the transitive closure and R* the reflexive transitive closure.
q_relation_closure_01.explanation: The only two-step chain adds (1,3); there are no further new positive-length reachable pairs. Since R has no cycle, R⁺ contains no diagonal pairs. R* unconditionally includes all three diagonals.
q_relation_closure_01.grading_criteria: Distinguish positive-length reachability from reachability allowing length zero. Give both closures and both cardinalities correctly.

q_relation_closure_02.title: Closures of the empty relation
q_relation_closure_02.statement: On A={a,b}, let R=∅. Which statement about its closures is correct?
q_relation_closure_02.explanation: The empty relation is already symmetric and transitive, so these closures remain empty. Reflexive closure must add both diagonal pairs, and reflexive transitive closure is also exactly I_A.
q_relation_closure_02.grading_criteria: Select B and explain that transitivity does not unconditionally require adding diagonal pairs.

options.text: The symmetric closure of R is I_A
The reflexive closure of R is empty

q_relation_closure_03.title: Generating an equivalence relation from required links
q_relation_closure_03.statement: Let A={a,b,c,d,e}, R={(a,b),(b,c),(d,e)}. Find the classes of the least equivalence relation containing R and its size.
q_relation_closure_03.answer_text: The classes are {a,b,c} and {d,e}; the equivalence relation has size 3²+2²=13.
q_relation_closure_03.explanation: Symmetry adds reverse edges; transitivity relates all of a,b,c and all of d,e; reflexivity supplies every diagonal. No requirement connects the two groups, so leastness excludes cross-group pairs.
q_relation_closure_03.grading_criteria: Explain why every pair within a group is related and no link between groups is required. Include each group's diagonals in the count.

q_relation_closure_04.title: Proving the equivalence-closure construction
q_relation_closure_04.statement: Let R be any relation on A and S=R∪R⁻¹. Prove that E=S*=I_A∪S∪S²∪… is the least equivalence relation containing R. Composition here is right to left.
q_relation_closure_04.answer_text: E contains R and I_A, so it is reflexive. Since S is symmetric, every S-chain can be reversed, so E is symmetric. Finite S-chains can be concatenated, including zero-length chains, so E is transitive. For any equivalence relation T containing R, symmetry gives S⊆T, reflexivity gives I_A⊆T, and repeated transitivity gives S^k⊆T. Thus E⊆T, proving leastness.
q_relation_closure_04.explanation: Prove both the three equivalence properties and leastness. Including I_A is necessary: an element completely isolated in S cannot be related to itself by a positive-length chain.
q_relation_closure_04.grading_criteria: Verify reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, and containment in every equivalence superrelation. Do not omit leastness or isolated elements.

q_function_mapping_01.title: Functions require totality and single-valuedness
q_function_mapping_01.statement: Let A={1,2}, B={a,b}. Which relations are functions from A to B?
q_function_mapping_01.explanation: A and D assign exactly one output to each input 1,2. B assigns two distinct outputs to 1 and fails single-valuedness. C gives no value for 2 and fails totality. D remains a valid function despite equal outputs for two inputs.
q_function_mapping_01.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,D; identify failure of single-valuedness in B and totality in C.

q_function_mapping_02.title: Counting functions and empty-set cases
q_function_mapping_02.statement: There are ____ functions from a 3-element set to a 2-element set, ____ functions from the empty set to that 2-element set, and ____ functions from a nonempty set to the empty set.
q_function_mapping_02.explanation: Each of three inputs independently chooses either of two outputs, giving 2³=8. An empty domain has no inputs requiring assignments, so the unique empty relation is a function. A nonempty domain has an input, but an empty codomain offers no value, so no function exists.
q_function_mapping_02.grading_criteria: All three blanks must be correct. Do not count zero functions for an empty domain or one function from a nonempty domain to the empty set.

q_function_mapping_03.title: Images and set preimages
q_function_mapping_03.statement: Let A={1,2,3,4}, B={0,1,2}. A function f:A→B sends odd inputs to 0 and even inputs to 1. Find f(A), f({1,4}), and f⁻¹[{1,2}].
q_function_mapping_03.explanation: Inputs 1,3 map to 0 and 2,4 to 1. The codomain element 2 has no preimage, but f is still valid. The preimage collects inputs actually mapping to 1 or 2, hence {2,4}.
q_function_mapping_03.grading_criteria: Write images as output sets and preimages as input sets. The codomain B is not the image.

q_function_mapping_04.title: Preimages preserve intersections; images need not
q_function_mapping_04.statement: Let f:A→B and S,T⊆B. Prove f⁻¹[S∩T]=f⁻¹[S]∩f⁻¹[T]. Then give a function and subsets U,V of A for which f(U∩V)=f(U)∩f(V) fails.
q_function_mapping_04.answer_text: For any x∈A, f(x)∈S∩T ⇔ f(x)∈S and f(x)∈T, equivalent to x belonging to both preimages. This proves the preimage equality. For a counterexample, let A={1,2}, B={a}, f(1)=f(2)=a, U={1}, V={2}. Then f(U∩V)=∅, but f(U)∩f(V)={a}.
q_function_mapping_04.explanation: Preimage membership keeps the same input x, so the intersection conditions match directly. In an intersection of images, the same output may come from different inputs in U and V, with none in U∩V.
q_function_mapping_04.grading_criteria: Give a bidirectional elementwise proof of the preimage equality. Specify the counterexample function and subsets and compute both unequal sides.

q_function_injection_01.title: Properties of an affine integer map
q_function_injection_01.statement: Define f:Z→Z by f(n)=2n+1. Is it injective, surjective, or bijective? Give reasons.
q_function_injection_01.answer_text: f is injective but not surjective, hence not bijective.
q_function_injection_01.explanation: If 2m+1=2n+1, then m=n, proving injectivity. All outputs are odd, so, for example, codomain element 0 is unattained. Thus f is not surjective and therefore not bijective.
q_function_injection_01.grading_criteria: Prove injectivity algebraically. Disprove surjectivity using a specific unattained integer and explain why it is unattained.

q_function_injection_02.title: Surjections from four elements to three
q_function_injection_02.statement: Let |A|=4 and |B|=3. How many surjections A→B are there? Explain your counting method.
q_function_injection_02.explanation: All three outputs must occur, so their preimage sizes must be 2,1,1. Choose the output used twice in 3 ways, its two inputs in C(4,2)=6 ways, and assign the remaining inputs to the other outputs in 2 ways. Total: 3×6×2=36.
q_function_injection_02.grading_criteria: Ensure every output occurs and avoid double-counting. Giving 3^4=81 without removing nonsurjections is incorrect.

q_function_injection_03.title: Existence constraints for finite sets
q_function_injection_03.statement: Let A={1,2,3}, B={a,b}. Which statements are correct?
q_function_injection_03.explanation: Three inputs into two outputs force a collision, ruling out injectivity. The assignment f(1)=a,f(2)=b,f(3)=b is surjective. The identity on A is bijective. Since A,B have different sizes, no bijection connects them.
q_function_injection_03.grading_criteria: Select exactly B,C. Justify nonexistence of an injection and give a reason or explicit construction for a surjection.

q_function_injection_04.title: Injectivity and surjectivity on finite sets of equal size
q_function_injection_04.statement: Let A,B each have n elements, with n finite, and let f:A→B. Prove f is injective if and only if surjective. Give an infinite-set example showing finiteness is necessary.
q_function_injection_04.answer_text: If f is injective, its n inputs give n distinct outputs. Since B has only n elements, all are attained, so f is surjective. If f were surjective but not injective, two inputs would coincide in value and its image would have at most n−1 elements, unable to cover B, a contradiction. For an infinite example, on N₀={0,1,2,…}, f(n)=n+1 is injective but misses 0 and is not surjective.
q_function_injection_04.explanation: Finite output counting is essential. For n=0 the unique empty function is both injective and surjective. Infinite sets can be bijective with proper subsets, so the finite 'one fewer output' argument does not apply.
q_function_injection_04.grading_criteria: Prove both directions, explicitly using finite equal cardinality. Give the domain, codomain, and an omitted element in the infinite example.

q_function_composition_01.title: Computing composition from tables
q_function_composition_01.statement: Let f:{1,2,3}→{a,b} have f(1)=a,f(2)=b,f(3)=a; let g:{a,b}→{0,1} have g(a)=1,g(b)=0. Find the table for g∘f.
q_function_composition_01.explanation: Looking up f first gives a,b,a; looking up those values in g gives 1,0,1. The composite has domain {1,2,3} and codomain {0,1}.
q_function_composition_01.grading_criteria: Give all three correct values and apply f before g. The letters a,b are intermediate, not final outputs.

q_function_composition_02.title: Composition is not commutative
q_function_composition_02.statement: On Z define f(n)=n+2 and g(n)=3n. Find (g∘f)(n) and (f∘g)(n), and decide whether the functions are equal.
q_function_composition_02.explanation: Adding 2 then multiplying by 3 gives 3(n+2)=3n+6. Multiplying by 3 then adding 2 gives 3n+2. Their outputs differ by 4 for every integer input.
q_function_composition_02.grading_criteria: Calculate both orders explicitly. Justify inequality using the expressions or a specific input.

q_function_composition_03.title: Types and identity functions
q_function_composition_03.statement: Given f:A→B, g:B→C, h:C→D, which statements hold for all such functions?
q_function_composition_03.explanation: Pointwise, either grouping gives h(g(f(a))), proving A. The two identities act on f's outputs and inputs without changing them, proving B,C. In f∘g, an output of g lies in C and need not belong to A, so D need not be defined.
q_function_composition_03.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,B,C. Explain that D can fail because the types do not match.

q_function_composition_04.title: Executing a modulo-five process twice
q_function_composition_04.statement: Reduce all numbers to representatives {0,1,2,3,4} modulo 5. Define f(x)=x+1 (mod5), g(x)=2x (mod5), and T=g∘f. Find T²(x) and all x satisfying T²(x)=x, where T²=T∘T.
q_function_composition_04.answer_text: T²(x)=4x+1 (mod5). The only solution is x=3.
q_function_composition_04.explanation: T(x)=2(x+1)=2x+2 (mod5). Applying it again gives 2(2x+2)+2=4x+6≡4x+1. Equating this to x gives 3x≡4(mod5). Since 3×2≡1, x≡8≡3. Indeed T(3)=3 and hence T²(3)=3; the other four representatives fail.
q_function_composition_04.grading_criteria: Treat T² as composition, not the numerical square of T(x). Solve modulo 5 and give representatives in the specified set.

q_function_inverse_01.title: The inverse table of a finite bijection
q_function_inverse_01.statement: Let A={a,b,c,d} and f:A→A satisfy f(a)=c,f(b)=a,f(c)=d,f(d)=b. Write the table of f⁻¹.
q_function_inverse_01.explanation: The four outputs cover A without repetition, so f is bijective. Find each output's unique source by reversing the four correspondences.
q_function_inverse_01.grading_criteria: Give all four inverse values and explain bijectivity. Do not interpret an inverse function as taking numerical reciprocals.

q_function_inverse_02.title: Codomains and existence of inverses
q_function_inverse_02.statement: Let f:Z→Z, f(n)=2n, and use f⁻¹[T] for the preimage of T. Which statements are correct?
q_function_inverse_02.explanation: The original f misses odd integers and is neither surjective nor bijective, so A fails. With codomain 2Z every output has exactly one preimage, proving B. The sources of 2,6 are 1,3, proving C. Preimages are defined for every function and do not imply a two-sided inverse, so D fails.
q_function_inverse_02.grading_criteria: Select exactly B,C and distinguish preimage notation f⁻¹[T] from a two-sided inverse function.

options.text: Changing the codomain to the even integers 2Z makes the rule bijective
If f⁻¹[{2,6}] is defined, the original f has a two-sided inverse

q_function_inverse_03.title: Inverse order for composite bijections
q_function_inverse_03.statement: Work modulo 7 on Z₇={0,1,2,3,4,5,6}. For f(x)=x+2, g(x)=3x, find a formula for (g∘f)⁻¹(y) and compute (g∘f)⁻¹(1).
q_function_inverse_03.explanation: The composite sends x to 3x+6. Since 3 has inverse 5 modulo 7, solving y≡3x+6 gives x≡5(y−6)≡5y+5. Alternatively apply g⁻¹(y)=5y then f⁻¹(z)=z−2, giving 5y−2≡5y+5. At y=1 this is 10≡3.
q_function_inverse_03.grading_criteria: Execute g⁻¹ before f⁻¹. Use modular arithmetic rather than ordinary division, and reduce the final value to a specified representative.

q_function_inverse_04.title: Left and right inverses must agree when both exist
q_function_inverse_04.statement: Let f:A→B, l:B→A, r:B→A satisfy l∘f=id_A and f∘r=id_B. Prove l=r and that f is bijective.
q_function_inverse_04.answer_text: By associativity, l=l∘id_B=l∘(f∘r)=(l∘f)∘r=id_A∘r=r. If f(a)=f(a′), applying l yields a=a′, so f is injective. For any b∈B, f(r(b))=b supplies a preimage, so f is surjective. Thus f is bijective and l=r=f⁻¹.
q_function_inverse_04.explanation: A left inverse guarantees injectivity; a right inverse guarantees surjectivity. Associativity joins them when both exist. The proof also covers empty sets whenever all the given functions exist.
q_function_inverse_04.grading_criteria: Prove equality of the inverses and separately establish injectivity and surjectivity. Keep the domains and codomains of all composites consistent.

q_set_operation_05.title: Set elements can themselves be sets
q_set_operation_05.statement: Let A={∅,{1}}. Which statements are correct?
q_set_operation_05.explanation: A has exactly the elements ∅ and {1}, proving A,B. The only element of {∅} belongs to A, proving C. The integer 1 itself is not an element of A, so D fails.
q_set_operation_05.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,B,C and distinguish set elements from integers nested inside them.

q_set_operation_06.title: Recovering subset counts from a power-set size
q_set_operation_06.statement: A finite set X satisfies |P(X)|=16. Then |X|=____, X has ____ nonempty subsets, and ____ nonempty proper subsets.
q_set_operation_06.explanation: 2^|X|=16=2⁴ gives |X|=4. Excluding ∅ from the 16 subsets leaves 15; excluding X as well leaves 14 nonempty proper subsets.
q_set_operation_06.grading_criteria: Identify the excluded objects. Nonempty and proper exclude two different subsets.

q_set_operation_07.title: An elementwise proof of De Morgan's law
q_set_operation_07.statement: Let A,B⊆U, with complements relative to the fixed universe U. Prove (A∩B)^c=A^c∪B^c.
q_set_operation_07.answer_text: For any x∈U, x∈(A∩B)^c means x does not belong to both A and B, equivalently x∉A or x∉B, equivalently x∈A^c∪B^c. Thus the sets are equal.
q_set_operation_07.explanation: The proof uses the equivalence of 'not both' with 'at least one not'. Restricting x to U matters because complements contain only elements of the universe.
q_set_operation_07.grading_criteria: Give the full bidirectional chain of equivalences and use the same U for all complements.

q_set_operation_08.title: Counting overlapping registrations for three activities
q_set_operation_08.statement: A class has 60 students. Activities A,B,C have 32,28,20 registrants, respectively. |A∩B|=15, |A∩C|=10, |B∩C|=8, and 5 register for all three. Find the numbers registering for at least one, exactly two, and none.
q_set_operation_08.answer_text: At least one: 52; exactly two: 18; none: 8.
q_set_operation_08.explanation: Inclusion-exclusion gives |A∪B∪C|=32+28+20−15−10−8+5=52. Each of the three pairwise intersections counts each triple registrant once, so exactly two gives 15+10+8−3×5=18. None gives 60−52=8.
q_set_operation_08.grading_criteria: Pairwise intersections include the triple intersection. For exactly two, subtract the triple intersection three times, not once.

q_relation_cartesian_05.title: Reading a relation matrix in row and column order
q_relation_cartesian_05.statement: A relation from A={u,v} to B={0,1,2} has rows u,v and columns 0,1,2, with rows (1,0,1),(0,1,0). List R and state the matrix dimensions of R⁻¹.
q_relation_cartesian_05.answer_text: R={(u,0),(u,2),(v,1)}. The matrix of R⁻¹ has 3 rows and 2 columns, the transpose of the original 2-by-3 matrix.
q_relation_cartesian_05.explanation: Each 1 corresponds to the ordered pair (row element,column element). Inverting makes B the source and A the target, exchanging row and column sets and changing 2×3 to 3×2.
q_relation_cartesian_05.grading_criteria: Match all three pairs to the specified ordering. Explain that inverse-matrix rows belong to B and columns to A.

q_relation_cartesian_06.title: Counting relations with required and forbidden edges
q_relation_cartesian_06.statement: Let A={0,1}, B={a,b,c}. Count relations A→B that must contain (0,a),(1,b) and must not contain (1,c).
q_relation_cartesian_06.explanation: A×B has 6 pairs. Three compatible conditions fix three pairs' inclusion states. The remaining three may each be included or excluded, giving 2³=8.
q_relation_cartesian_06.grading_criteria: This is a general relation, with no single-value condition per row. Distinguish the three fixed conditions from the three free choices.

q_relation_cartesian_07.title: Equal product cardinalities do not imply equal sets
q_relation_cartesian_07.statement: Does A×B=B×A hold for all sets A,B? Give the simplest nonempty counterexample and explain why finite products nevertheless have equal cardinalities.
q_relation_cartesian_07.answer_text: No. Let A={0}, B={1}. Then A×B={(0,1)} and B×A={(1,0)}, which differ. For finite sets, their sizes are |A||B| and |B||A|, equal by commutativity of integer multiplication.
q_relation_cartesian_07.explanation: Order affects an ordered pair's identity; cardinality records only quantity. Equal sets have equal cardinality, but the converse fails.
q_relation_cartesian_07.grading_criteria: Give two distinct ordered pairs in the counterexample and distinguish equality of sets from equality of cardinalities.

q_relation_cartesian_08.title: Each member participates in at least one task
q_relation_cartesian_08.statement: There are 2 labeled members and 3 labeled tasks. Members may participate in several tasks and tasks may have several members. How many member–task participation relations make each member participate in at least one task?
q_relation_cartesian_08.explanation: Each member may choose any nonempty subset of the three tasks, giving 2³−1=7 choices. Independent choices for the two members give 7²=49. Unassigned tasks are allowed, so columns need not be nonempty.
q_relation_cartesian_08.grading_criteria: Explain the nonempty task-subset choice for each member. Do not count functions as 3² or add an unstated task-coverage condition.

q_relation_operation_05.title: Two-stage relations from users through groups to resources
q_relation_operation_05.statement: Let A={Alpha,Beta}, B={readers,editors}, C={document,chart}. Let R={(Alpha,readers),(Beta,editors)} and S={(readers,document),(editors,document),(editors,chart)}. Find S∘R, applying R before S, and explain each pair.
q_relation_operation_05.explanation: Alpha reaches the document through the readers group. Beta reaches the document and chart through the editors group. The composition gives only access links implied by the supplied relations; no inheritance between readers and editors is assumed.
q_relation_operation_05.grading_criteria: List all three pairs and identify groups as the intermediate elements. Do not add (Alpha,chart).

q_relation_operation_06.title: Periodicity of powers of a 3-cycle
q_relation_operation_06.statement: Let A={0,1,2}, R={(0,1),(1,2),(2,0)}. Find R⁰,R³,R⁴ and R^(3k) for every integer k≥0.
q_relation_operation_06.explanation: Every three steps around the directed cycle return to the starting point, and every vertex has a unique successor. Thus the three-step relation is exactly the identity and four steps equal one additional step. The case k=0 follows from the definition of R⁰.
q_relation_operation_06.grading_criteria: Include the zero-power boundary case and note that relation powers allow repeated vertices.

q_relation_operation_07.title: Composition need not distribute over intersection
q_relation_operation_07.statement: On A={1,2,3,4}, let R₁={(1,2)}, R₂={(1,3)}, S={(2,4),(3,4)}, with composition right to left. Compute S∘(R₁∩R₂) and (S∘R₁)∩(S∘R₂), and decide whether they are always equal.
q_relation_operation_07.answer_text: The first is ∅; the second is {(1,4)}. They are not equal in general.
q_relation_operation_07.explanation: R₁,R₂ have no common edge, so the left side is empty. The right-side compositions use different intermediates 2 and 3, but both produce (1,4), which remains in their intersection.
q_relation_operation_07.grading_criteria: Explicitly give both results and explain that the two compositions may use different intermediate elements.

q_relation_operation_08.title: Inverses, unions, intersections, and composition
q_relation_operation_08.statement: Let R,S be relations on the same set A, with composition right to left. Which identities always hold?
q_relation_operation_08.explanation: Inversion swaps the components of every pair, preserving union and intersection; applying it twice restores R. Inverting a composition must reverse order: (R∘S)⁻¹=S⁻¹∘R⁻¹. Thus C is not always true.
q_relation_operation_08.grading_criteria: Select exactly A,B,D and give the corrected reversed-order formula for C.

q_relation_property_07.title: Assessing all properties of a finite relation
q_relation_property_07.statement: Let A={1,2,3}, R={(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,1)}. Determine whether R is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, and transitive, with reasons for each.
q_relation_property_07.answer_text: It is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, but not antisymmetric.
q_relation_property_07.explanation: All diagonal pairs are present, proving reflexivity. The only off-diagonal link is between 1 and 2 and appears both ways, proving symmetry. Since 1R2 and 2R1 with 1≠2, antisymmetry fails. Links stay within {1,2} or the singleton {3}, and every within-block pair is present, so the endpoints of every two-step chain are linked; R is transitive.
q_relation_property_07.grading_criteria: Give all four conclusions with justification. A visual impression alone does not establish transitivity.

q_relation_property_05.title: Characterizing relations that are symmetric and antisymmetric
q_relation_property_05.statement: Prove that a relation R on A is both symmetric and antisymmetric if and only if R⊆I_A, where I_A={(a,a)｜a∈A}.
q_relation_property_05.answer_text: If both properties hold, any aRb gives bRa by symmetry, then a=b by antisymmetry. Hence R⊆I_A. Conversely, if R contains only diagonal pairs, every edge is its own reverse, so R is symmetric; every bidirectional link has identical endpoints, so R is antisymmetric.
q_relation_property_05.explanation: R may omit some or even all diagonal pairs, so reflexivity is not required. The empty relation is included.
q_relation_property_05.grading_criteria: Prove both directions. Do not strengthen R⊆I_A to R=I_A in the converse.

q_relation_property_06.title: Bidirectional edges force loops
q_relation_property_06.statement: Let A={a,b}, R={(a,b),(b,a)}. Is R transitive? Keeping both pairs, which pairs must at least be added to make it transitive?
q_relation_property_06.answer_text: R is not transitive. Add at least (a,a),(b,b); the resulting A×A is transitive.
q_relation_property_06.explanation: aRb and bRa require aRa; the reversed two-step chain requires bRb. Once all four pairs of A×A are present, the endpoints of any two-step chain are related.
q_relation_property_06.grading_criteria: State that elements may repeat in the transitivity test and prove the completed relation is transitive.

q_relation_property_08.title: Counting reflexive symmetric and reflexive antisymmetric relations
q_relation_property_08.statement: On a 3-element set A, how many relations are reflexive and symmetric? How many are reflexive and antisymmetric? Do not additionally require transitivity.
q_relation_property_08.answer_text: There are 8 reflexive symmetric relations and 27 reflexive antisymmetric relations.
q_relation_property_08.explanation: Reflexivity fixes all three diagonal pairs as present. Each of the three unordered pairs of distinct elements gives two opposite edges. Symmetry permits both or neither, yielding 2³=8. Antisymmetry permits neither, only one direction, or only the other, yielding 3³=27.
q_relation_property_08.grading_criteria: Make clear that transitivity is not required, so the three off-diagonal groups are independent. Antisymmetry does not force one direction to be chosen.

q_relation_equivalence_05.title: Recovering a relation from two partition blocks
q_relation_equivalence_05.statement: The partition of A={1,2,3,4,5} is {{1,3},{2,4,5}}. Declare elements equivalent when they lie in the same block. Decide whether (1,2),(4,5) belong to R and find |R|.
q_relation_equivalence_05.explanation: 1 and 2 lie in different blocks, while 4 and 5 lie in the same block. The first block contributes 2²=4 ordered pairs and the second 3²=9, for a total of 13.
q_relation_equivalence_05.grading_criteria: Use the same-block condition to decide links. Count diagonals and both directions between distinct elements.

q_relation_equivalence_06.title: From the modulo-four quotient to the modulo-two quotient
q_relation_equivalence_06.statement: Take quotient sets of Z by congruence modulo 4 and modulo 2. Is F([a]₄)=[a]₂ well-defined? Is F injective or surjective? Explain.
q_relation_equivalence_06.answer_text: It is well-defined and surjective, but not injective.
q_relation_equivalence_06.explanation: If [a]₄=[b]₄, then 4∣(a−b), hence 2∣(a−b), so [a]₂=[b]₂. The result is independent of representatives. The two modulo-2 classes are images of [0]₄,[1]₄, proving surjectivity. Distinct inputs [0]₄,[2]₄ both map to [0]₂, disproving injectivity.
q_relation_equivalence_06.grading_criteria: First check representative independence, then give coverage for surjectivity and two distinct input classes witnessing noninjectivity.

q_relation_equivalence_07.title: A union of equivalence relations need not be an equivalence relation
q_relation_equivalence_07.statement: On A={1,2,3}, let R correspond to {{1,2},{3}} and S to {{1},{2,3}}. Must R∪S be an equivalence relation? Identify the specific property that fails here.
q_relation_equivalence_07.answer_text: Here R∪S is not an equivalence relation: it is not transitive, since (1,2),(2,3) are present but (1,3) is absent.
q_relation_equivalence_07.explanation: Each partition defines an equivalence relation. Union retains every diagonal and symmetry, but edges from different relations may form a two-step chain missing its direct endpoint link.
q_relation_equivalence_07.grading_criteria: Identify transitivity as the failing property and give the three-element witness. Merely saying 'not necessarily' is insufficient.

q_relation_equivalence_08.title: Exactly two equivalence classes on three elements
q_relation_equivalence_08.statement: On A={a,b,c}, how many equivalence relations have exactly two classes? How many ordered pairs does each contain?
q_relation_equivalence_08.answer_text: There are 3 such equivalence relations, each with 5 ordered pairs.
q_relation_equivalence_08.explanation: The two nonempty blocks must have sizes 1 and 2. Choose the singleton in 3 ways, uniquely determining the other block. Each relation has size 1²+2²=5.
q_relation_equivalence_08.grading_criteria: Count unordered partitions; do not count a swap of block order as a new partition.

q_relation_order_05.title: Recognizing a total order
q_relation_order_05.statement: With the specified relation on each given set, which is a totally ordered set?
q_relation_order_05.explanation: In {1,2,4,8}, every pair is comparable by divisibility, which is a partial order. The other options contain incomparable pairs: 2,3; {a},{b}; and 2,3, respectively.
q_relation_order_05.grading_criteria: Select A and give an incomparable pair from at least one other option.

q_relation_order_06.title: Lexicographic and componentwise orders
q_relation_order_06.statement: On Z×Z, define (a,b)≤_L(c,d) if a<c, or a=c and b≤d. Define (a,b)≤_P(c,d) if a≤c and b≤d. Explain why the former is a total order and the latter is not.
q_relation_order_06.answer_text: Lexicographic order is a total order. Componentwise order is a partial order but is not total.
q_relation_order_06.explanation: Lexicographic order is reflexive. Comparisons both ways force equality of first components and then second components, proving antisymmetry. In two successive comparisons, if either first component strictly increases, the first component increases from start to finish; otherwise all three first components agree and transitivity of second components applies. Any two pairs are comparable by first comparing first components, then second components if needed. Componentwise order inherits all three partial-order properties in each component, but neither direction compares (0,1) and (1,0), so it is not total.
q_relation_order_06.grading_criteria: Establish lexicographic partial-order properties and comparability of every pair separately. Give an explicit incomparable pair for componentwise order.

q_relation_order_07.title: Bounds must lie in the given poset
q_relation_order_07.statement: Order A={2,3,6,12,18} by divisibility. For S={2,3}, find all upper and lower bounds and the least upper bound. Does a greatest lower bound exist?
q_relation_order_07.answer_text: Upper bounds are {6,12,18}; there are no lower bounds. The least upper bound is 6; no greatest lower bound exists.
q_relation_order_07.explanation: Upper bounds must be divisible by both 2 and 3, giving precisely 6,12,18 in A, and 6 divides the others. Their only positive common divisor is 1, outside A, so the lower-bound set in A is empty; 1 cannot be used as an infimum.
q_relation_order_07.grading_criteria: All bounds must belong to A. Distinguish existence of an integer gcd from existence of an infimum in the given poset.

q_relation_order_08.title: Linear arrangements respecting a partial order
q_relation_order_08.statement: Order A={1,2,3,6} by divisibility. Arrange the four elements in a row so that whenever a strictly divides b, a appears to the left of b. How many arrangements are there? List them.
q_relation_order_08.explanation: 1 must precede the other three, and 6 must follow them. The incomparable elements 2,3 can appear in either order, leaving exactly two arrangements.
q_relation_order_08.grading_criteria: Respect every transitive constraint and do not impose an extra order on incomparable 2,3.

q_relation_closure_05.title: Order of applying two basic closures
q_relation_closure_05.statement: Let r(R)=R∪I_A be reflexive closure and s(R)=R∪R⁻¹ symmetric closure. Prove r(s(R))=s(r(R)).
q_relation_closure_05.explanation: Inversion preserves unions and fixes I_A, so adding loops and adding reverse edges give the same result in either order.
q_relation_closure_05.grading_criteria: Explicitly use (R∪I_A)⁻¹=R⁻¹∪I_A. This conclusion concerns these two closures only; it does not establish that all closures commute.

q_relation_closure_06.title: Reachability on four points and a Boolean matrix
q_relation_closure_06.statement: Let A={1,2,3,4}, R={(1,2),(2,4),(1,3),(3,4)}. Find R⁺ and its 0–1 matrix with rows and columns ordered 1,2,3,4.
q_relation_closure_06.explanation: 1 reaches 4 through either 2 or 3, so only (1,4) is added, once. There are no directed cycles, so no diagonal pairs occur in positive-length transitive closure, and 4 reaches no element.
q_relation_closure_06.grading_criteria: List the five pairs and orient the matrix correctly. Two different chains from 1 to 4 do not justify a matrix entry of 2.

q_relation_closure_07.title: Idempotence of transitive closure
q_relation_closure_07.statement: Write t(R) for the transitive closure of R. Prove t(t(R))=t(R).
q_relation_closure_07.answer_text: Let T=t(R). Since T is already transitive, T itself is a transitive relation containing T. The least such relation t(T) is therefore contained in T. The closure definition also gives T⊆t(T). Together these imply t(T)=T.
q_relation_closure_07.explanation: Closure takes the least qualifying superrelation in one operation, rather than adding arbitrary edges repeatedly. Reapplying the same closure after completion changes nothing.
q_relation_closure_07.grading_criteria: Use both transitivity of T and the requirement that a closure contain its original relation to prove both inclusions.

q_relation_closure_08.title: Closure sizes from a cycle and a terminal vertex
q_relation_closure_08.statement: On A={1,2,3,4}, let R={(1,2),(2,3),(3,1),(3,4)}. Find |R⁺| and |R*| and explain their difference.
q_relation_closure_08.explanation: Vertices 1,2,3 form a directed cycle. Each reaches 1,2,3 by positive-length walks and also reaches 4 through 3, giving 3×4=12 pairs. Vertex 4 has no outgoing edges and cannot reach any vertex, including itself, in positive length. R* adds only (4,4), giving 13.
q_relation_closure_08.grading_criteria: Do not add (4,4) unconditionally to R⁺ or omit the loops generated by closed walks at 1,2,3.

q_function_mapping_05.title: Totality after changing the domain
q_function_mapping_05.statement: Let Γ={(a,0),(b,0)}. Is this a function graph from {a,b} to {0,1}? Does it remain so if the domain becomes {a,b,c} without changing Γ? What if only the codomain becomes {0}?
q_function_mapping_05.answer_text: Yes from {a,b} to {0,1}; no with domain {a,b,c}; yes from {a,b} to {0}.
q_function_mapping_05.explanation: Both original domain elements have unique outputs. In the enlarged domain, c has no value, violating totality. The smaller codomain {0} still contains every actual output, so the relation remains a function.
q_function_mapping_05.grading_criteria: Discuss totality, single-valuedness, and membership of outputs in the codomain separately. The unused original codomain element 1 is not a defect.

q_function_mapping_06.title: Counting functions with fixed or unequal values
q_function_mapping_06.statement: Let A={a,b,c,d}, B={0,1,2}. Separately count functions with f(a)=0 and functions with f(a)≠f(b). These are separate requirements, not simultaneous ones.
q_function_mapping_06.explanation: For the first condition, fix a's output and independently choose the others in 3³=27 ways. For the second, choose a's output in 3 ways, a different output for b in 2 ways, and each of c,d in 3 ways: 3×2×3×3=54.
q_function_mapping_06.grading_criteria: Treat the conditions separately; do not carry f(a)=0 into the second count.

q_function_mapping_07.title: Does a department register define a function?
q_function_mapping_07.statement: Let employees E={Alpha,Beta,Gamma} and departments D={research,operations}. The register is {(Alpha,research),(Beta,operations),(Gamma,research)}. Is it a function E→D? What changes if (Alpha,operations) is added?
q_function_mapping_07.answer_text: The original register is a function; after adding (Alpha,operations), it is not.
q_function_mapping_07.explanation: Originally every employee has exactly one department. Alpha and Gamma sharing research does not violate single-valuedness. The added pair gives Alpha two different values, research and operations, violating the function definition.
q_function_mapping_07.grading_criteria: Distinguish different inputs sharing an output from the same input having two distinct outputs.

q_function_mapping_08.title: What does taking a preimage and then an image recover?
q_function_mapping_08.statement: For f:A→B and T⊆B, prove f(f⁻¹[T])=T∩f(A), where f⁻¹[T] denotes only a preimage set.
q_function_mapping_08.answer_text: If y∈f(f⁻¹[T]), some x∈A has y=f(x) and f(x)∈T, so y∈T∩f(A). Conversely, if y∈T∩f(A), some x∈A satisfies f(x)=y. Since y∈T, x∈f⁻¹[T], hence y∈f(f⁻¹[T]).
q_function_mapping_08.explanation: An unattained codomain element has no preimage even if it belongs to T, so the left side cannot generally be replaced by all of T.
q_function_mapping_08.grading_criteria: Prove both inclusions and state that no inverse function is required. Explain why intersection with f(A) is necessary.

q_function_injection_05.title: Restricting an injection's domain
q_function_injection_05.statement: Let f:A→B be injective and S⊆A. Prove the restriction f|_S:S→B remains injective. Does further changing the codomain to f(S) give a bijection?
q_function_injection_05.answer_text: The restriction remains injective; regarded as S→f(S), it is bijective.
q_function_injection_05.explanation: For x,y∈S, equality f|_S(x)=f|_S(y) means f(x)=f(y), so injectivity on A gives x=y. By definition every element of f(S) comes from S, making the restricted map surjective onto the new codomain. Together these give a bijection, even for empty S.
q_function_injection_05.grading_criteria: Explain that restriction leaves the rule unchanged. Surjectivity holds relative to f(S), not necessarily the original B.

q_function_injection_06.title: The remainder map covers its codomain
q_function_injection_06.statement: Let f:Z→{0,1,2} send each integer to its nonnegative remainder on division by 3. Prove surjectivity and decide injectivity.
q_function_injection_06.answer_text: f is surjective but not injective.
q_function_injection_06.explanation: Inputs 0,1,2 attain all three codomain elements, proving surjectivity. Distinct inputs 0 and 3 both map to 0, disproving injectivity. Negative integers use their unique nonnegative remainders and do not affect the conclusion.
q_function_injection_06.grading_criteria: Cover all three target values for surjectivity and give two distinct inputs with equal value for noninjectivity.

q_function_injection_07.title: What follows from an injective or surjective composite?
q_function_injection_07.statement: Let f:A→B, g:B→C. Prove that injectivity of g∘f implies injectivity of f, and surjectivity of g∘f implies surjectivity of g. Must the other conclusions, 'g is injective' and 'f is surjective', hold? Give examples.
q_function_injection_07.answer_text: The first two implications hold; the other two need not. A common counterexample is A={1}, B={a,b}, C={0}, f(1)=a, g(a)=g(b)=0.
q_function_injection_07.explanation: If f(x)=f(y), applying g gives equal composite values, whose injectivity yields x=y. If the composite is surjective, any c∈C has a∈A with g(f(a))=c, so b=f(a) is a preimage under g. In the counterexample the singleton-to-singleton composite is both injective and surjective, but g is not injective and f is not surjective.
q_function_injection_07.grading_criteria: Prove both necessary implications and specify every domain, codomain, and value in the counterexample.

q_function_injection_08.title: Finite counts of injections and bijections
q_function_injection_08.statement: How many injections go from a labeled 2-element set to a labeled 4-element set? How many bijections connect two labeled 4-element sets?
q_function_injection_08.explanation: For an injection the first input has 4 output choices and the second has 3 unused choices, giving 4×3=12. A bijection successively uses four distinct outputs in 4×3×2×1=24 ways.
q_function_injection_08.grading_criteria: Both inputs and outputs are labeled; do not divide by a permutation count. The two inputs of an injection must have different values.

q_function_composition_05.title: Checking the domain of a composite expression
q_function_composition_05.statement: Let f:Z→Z, f(n)=n², and g:{1,2,3,…}→Z, g(m)=m+1. Does g(f(n)) directly define a function on all of Z? If not, give the largest allowable input subset and its formula.
q_function_composition_05.answer_text: No. The largest allowable input subset is Z\{0}, on which the formula is n²+1.
q_function_composition_05.explanation: At n=0, f(n)=0 lies outside g's positive-integer domain, so the second step is undefined. Every nonzero integer has a positive square, so every other input is allowed.
q_function_composition_05.grading_criteria: Check intermediate values, not only algebraic substitution. Do not omit negative integers from the largest input subset.

q_function_composition_06.title: A pointwise proof of associativity
q_function_composition_06.statement: Given f:A→B, g:B→C, h:C→D, prove (h∘g)∘f=h∘(g∘f) and state the domain and codomain of both sides.
q_function_composition_06.answer_text: Both sides have type A→D. For any a∈A, the left side is (h∘g)(f(a))=h(g(f(a))); the right side is h((g∘f)(a))=h(g(f(a))). They agree at every a and are equal.
q_function_composition_06.explanation: Associativity changes grouping only, preserving the execution order f,g,h. The given types make every substitution valid.
q_function_composition_06.grading_criteria: Give the common type and compare an arbitrary input pointwise. A single numerical example is insufficient.

q_function_composition_07.title: A particular commuting pair: rotation and bitwise complement
q_function_composition_07.statement: Let A consist of all 3-bit binary strings. Define left rotation r(abc)=bca and bitwise complement h(abc)=(1−a)(1−b)(1−c). Decide whether h∘r=r∘h and compute both on 100.
q_function_composition_07.answer_text: The composites are equal and both send 100 to 110.
q_function_composition_07.explanation: Rotating then complementing gives (1−b)(1−c)(1−a); complementing then rotating gives the same string for every input. Specifically, r(100)=001, whose complement is 110; h(100)=011, whose rotation is also 110.
q_function_composition_07.grading_criteria: Compare a general three-bit string; agreement at 100 alone does not prove equality of functions. Execute both compositions in the correct order.

q_function_composition_08.title: Iteration period of a cyclic shift
q_function_composition_08.statement: On Z₆={0,1,2,3,4,5}, let f(x)=x+2 (mod6). Find f^k(x) for k≥0 and the least positive k with f^k=id.
q_function_composition_08.answer_text: f^k(x)=x+2k (mod6); the least positive k is 3.
q_function_composition_08.explanation: Every application adds 2, so k applications add 2k, with k=0 giving the identity. Restoring every input requires 2k≡0(mod6), equivalent to 3∣k; the least positive choice is 3.
q_function_composition_08.grading_criteria: Find when the whole function is the identity, not just a single input. Require k to be positive.

q_function_inverse_05.title: A one-sided inverse need not be two-sided
q_function_inverse_05.statement: Let N₀={0,1,2,…}. For f:N₀→N₀, f(n)=n+1, define l(0)=0 and l(n)=n−1 for n≥1. Verify l is a left inverse but not two-sided. For h:Z→N₀, h(n)=|n|, give a right inverse and show it is not two-sided.
q_function_inverse_05.answer_text: l∘f=id_N₀, but f(l(0))=1≠0. For h take r:N₀→Z, r(k)=k. Then h∘r=id_N₀, but r(h(−1))=1≠−1. Thus neither inverse is two-sided.
q_function_inverse_05.explanation: In the first example f misses 0, so a left inverse cannot repair surjectivity. In the second h is not injective, and the right inverse selects nonnegative sources without restoring both positive and negative inputs.
q_function_inverse_05.grading_criteria: For both examples check the identity in the correct direction and give a specific input where the other direction fails.

q_function_inverse_06.title: Proving the reversed-order inverse law
q_function_inverse_06.statement: Let f:A→B and g:B→C be bijections. Prove (g∘f)⁻¹=f⁻¹∘g⁻¹ and check the type of the right side.
q_function_inverse_06.answer_text: The type of f⁻¹∘g⁻¹ is C→A. Set H=f⁻¹∘g⁻¹. Then H∘(g∘f)=f⁻¹∘(g⁻¹∘g)∘f=id_A, and (g∘f)∘H=g∘(f∘f⁻¹)∘g⁻¹=id_C. Thus H is the required two-sided inverse.
q_function_inverse_06.explanation: The inverse first uses g⁻¹ to restore an output in C to B, then f⁻¹ to restore it to A, reversing the original process.
q_function_inverse_06.grading_criteria: Check both identity equations and the type C→A. The intuition of 'working backward' alone is insufficient.

q_function_inverse_07.title: A self-inverse bijection modulo eight
q_function_inverse_07.statement: On Z₈={0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}, let f(x)=3x+2 (mod8). Find f⁻¹ and decide whether f equals its inverse.
q_function_inverse_07.explanation: Since 3×3≡1(mod8), y≡3x+2 gives x≡3(y−2)≡3y+2. Alternatively f(f(x))=3(3x+2)+2=9x+8≡x directly proves that f is bijective and self-inverse.
q_function_inverse_07.grading_criteria: Use the inverse of 3 modulo 8 and simplify the constant. Verify or justify a two-sided inverse; do not divide by 3 as a real number.

q_function_inverse_08.title: Preimage sets versus inverse relations
q_function_inverse_08.statement: Let f:{1,2,3}→{a,b}, with f(1)=f(2)=a,f(3)=b. Find the preimage set f⁻¹[{a}] and list the inverse relation of the function graph. Is that relation a function from {a,b} to {1,2,3}?
q_function_inverse_08.answer_text: The preimage is {1,2}. The inverse relation is {(a,1),(a,2),(b,3)}, which is not a function.
q_function_inverse_08.explanation: A set preimage may contain several inputs, so {1,2} is valid. Reversing the graph gives input a two outputs, 1 and 2, violating single-valuedness. The original f is not injective and has no two-sided inverse function.
q_function_inverse_08.grading_criteria: Distinguish a set from a relation consisting of ordered pairs, and explicitly identify a's two distinct outputs.

q_algebra_group_01.title: Recognizing subgroups of a modular additive group
q_algebra_group_01.statement: In the additive group (ℤ₈,+), which subset is a subgroup? All addition is modulo 8.
q_algebra_group_01.explanation: The four even residue classes {0,2,4,6} are closed under addition modulo 8 and include 0. Elements 0,4 are self-inverse, while 2,6 are inverses. The other subsets fail closure or omit 0.
q_algebra_group_01.grading_criteria: Select A and explain closure, identity, and inverses, or apply a subgroup criterion.

q_algebra_group_02.title: Element order and a generated subgroup
q_algebra_group_02.statement: In (ℤ₁₂,+), find the order of 4 and list the cyclic subgroup it generates.
q_algebra_group_02.explanation: Repeated addition gives 4,8,12≡0(mod12), first returning to 0 after 3 additions. All integer multiples of 4 modulo 12 yield only 0,4,8. The formula 12/gcd(12,4)=3 provides a check.
q_algebra_group_02.grading_criteria: Explain why 3 is the least positive number of additions and list three distinct elements. The value 4 is not its order.

q_algebra_group_03.title: Groups in which every element is self-inverse
q_algebra_group_03.statement: Let G be a group with g²=e for every g∈G. Prove G is abelian.
q_algebra_group_03.answer_text: Every element equals its inverse. Thus ab=(ab)⁻¹=b⁻¹a⁻¹=ba, so G is abelian.
q_algebra_group_03.explanation: From g²=e we get g⁻¹=g. For any a,b∈G, ab also belongs to G, so (ab)⁻¹=ab. The inverse-product law also gives (ab)⁻¹=b⁻¹a⁻¹=ba. Hence ab=ba.
q_algebra_group_03.grading_criteria: Apply the hypothesis to a,b, and ab, and use the reversed-order inverse-product formula correctly.

q_algebra_group_04.title: When does a closed subset automatically form a subgroup?
q_algebra_group_04.statement: Prove that every nonempty multiplicatively closed subset H of a finite group G is a subgroup. Give a nonempty closed subset of an infinite group that is not a subgroup.
q_algebra_group_04.answer_text: In the finite case, positive powers of any a∈H repeat. Some positive power is therefore e, giving both e and a⁻¹ in H, so H is a subgroup. For an infinite counterexample, use the positive integers in (ℤ,+).
q_algebra_group_04.explanation: For a∈H, closure puts a,a²,… in finite H, so aⁱ=aʲ for some 1≤i<j. Cancel in G to get a^(j−i)=e, hence e∈H. If j−i=1 then a=e and its inverse is e; otherwise a^(j−i−1)∈H is its inverse. This works for every a; associativity is inherited from G. In (ℤ,+), H={1,2,3,…} is nonempty and closed under addition, but lacks 0 and additive inverses.
q_algebra_group_04.grading_criteria: Derive the identity from repeating powers and then derive inverses. For the counterexample verify closure and identify the failing group axioms.

q_algebra_group_05.title: Proving the standard subgroup criterion
q_algebra_group_05.statement: Let H be a nonempty subset of a group G with ab⁻¹∈H for every a,b∈H. Prove H is a subgroup of G.
q_algebra_group_05.answer_text: Choose a∈H to get aa⁻¹=e∈H. Then eb⁻¹ gives closure under inverses. Finally apply the criterion with b⁻¹ in place of b to get ab∈H.
q_algebra_group_05.explanation: Nonemptiness supplies a∈H and hence aa⁻¹=e∈H. For b∈H, the criterion on e,b yields b⁻¹∈H. For a,b∈H, use the newly obtained b⁻¹∈H to get a(b⁻¹)⁻¹=ab∈H. Thus H contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses; associativity is inherited from G.
q_algebra_group_05.grading_criteria: Derive identity, inverses, and product closure in a complete logical order, using nonemptiness explicitly.

q_algebra_group_06.title: Finding all generators of a cyclic additive group
q_algebra_group_06.statement: Find all generators of the additive group ℤ₁₀, and explain why 2 is not a generator.
q_algebra_group_06.answer_text: The generators are 1,3,7,9. The order of 2 is 5, and it generates only {0,2,4,6,8}.
q_algebra_group_06.explanation: The order of a in ℤ₁₀ is 10/gcd(10,a). It equals 10 exactly when gcd(10,a)=1, giving 1,3,7,9. For a=2 the order is 10/2=5, and its multiples give only the five even residue classes, not the whole group.
q_algebra_group_06.grading_criteria: List every generator and give the coprimality criterion. Use the order or generated subgroup to explain why 2 fails.

q_algebra_group_07.title: Cancellation in a group without commutativity
q_algebra_group_07.statement: Let G be a group and a,b,c∈G satisfy ab=ac. Without assuming G is abelian, prove b=c and specify on which side to multiply by the inverse.
q_algebra_group_07.answer_text: Multiply both sides on the left by a⁻¹. Associativity gives (a⁻¹a)b=(a⁻¹a)c, hence b=c.
q_algebra_group_07.explanation: The common factor a is on the left, so left-multiply: a⁻¹(ab)=a⁻¹(ac). Associativity gives (a⁻¹a)b=(a⁻¹a)c, or eb=ec, hence b=c. No factors are reordered, so commutativity is unnecessary.
q_algebra_group_07.grading_criteria: Explicitly left-multiply by the inverse and use associativity and the identity. Right-multiplying and directly canceling would not justify the result.

q_algebra_group_08.title: Is the group of units modulo eight cyclic?
q_algebra_group_08.statement: Let U={1,3,5,7} under multiplication modulo 8. Explain why U is a group and determine whether it is cyclic.
q_algebra_group_08.answer_text: U is an abelian group of four elements, but is not cyclic. Every nonidentity element has order 2.
q_algebra_group_08.explanation: U consists of all units of ℤ₈, so multiplication is closed; associativity is inherited from modular integer multiplication, and the identity is 1. Direct calculation gives 3²≡5²≡7²≡1(mod8), supplying inverses. All three nonidentity elements have order 2, so none has order 4 and none generates the whole group.
q_algebra_group_08.grading_criteria: Explain the group conditions and inverses. Four elements alone do not imply cyclicity; rule it out using element orders.

q_algebra_homomorphism_01.title: The kernel of a reduction map
q_algebra_homomorphism_01.statement: For additive groups, define φ:ℤ₆→ℤ₃ by φ([x]₆)=[x]₃. Which set is its kernel?
q_algebra_homomorphism_01.explanation: The kernel consists of domain elements mapping to 0 in ℤ₃. Among representatives 0 through 5, exactly 0 and 3 are divisible by 3, so the kernel is {[0]₆,[3]₆}. Representatives differing by 6 are also congruent modulo 3, proving well-definedness.
q_algebra_homomorphism_01.grading_criteria: Select C. Kernel elements must belong to the domain ℤ₆.

q_algebra_homomorphism_02.title: Kernel and image of a multiplication homomorphism
q_algebra_homomorphism_02.statement: On the additive group modulo 8, define φ:ℤ₈→ℤ₈ by φ(x)=2x(mod8). Prove it is a homomorphism, find its kernel and image, and decide whether it is an isomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_02.answer_text: It is a homomorphism, with kernel {0,4} and image {0,2,4,6}. It is not an isomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_02.explanation: φ(x+y)=2(x+y)≡2x+2y=φ(x)+φ(y)(mod8), so addition is preserved. The kernel condition 2x≡0(mod8) is equivalent to x≡0(mod4), giving 0,4 in ℤ₈. Doubling representatives 0 through 7 gives exactly 0,2,4,6. The nontrivial kernel prevents injectivity and the proper image prevents surjectivity, so it is not an isomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_02.grading_criteria: Correctly verify the homomorphism property, kernel, image, and isomorphism decision using injectivity and surjectivity.

q_algebra_homomorphism_03.title: Using structure rather than cardinality alone
q_algebra_homomorphism_03.statement: Which statements about group homomorphisms and isomorphisms are correct?
q_algebra_homomorphism_03.explanation: Isomorphisms preserve element orders. In ℤ₄, 1 has order 4, while every nonidentity element of ℤ₂×ℤ₂ has order 2, so B holds. A homomorphism's kernel is a subgroup of its domain, so C holds. Equal cardinality does not ensure isomorphism, and an arbitrary bijection need not preserve the operation.
q_algebra_homomorphism_03.grading_criteria: Select only B,C. Explicitly identify element order as an isomorphism invariant.

options.text: Two finite groups with equally many elements must be isomorphic.
ℤ₄ and ℤ₂×ℤ₂ are not isomorphic because their element-order distributions differ.
The kernel of a group homomorphism is a subgroup of the domain group.
Every bijection between two groups is a group isomorphism.

q_algebra_homomorphism_04.title: The kernel criterion for injectivity
q_algebra_homomorphism_04.statement: Let φ:G→H be a group homomorphism. Prove φ is injective if and only if kerφ={e_G}.
q_algebra_homomorphism_04.answer_text: If φ is injective, only e_G maps to e_H. Conversely, if the kernel is trivial and φ(a)=φ(b), then φ(ab⁻¹)=e_H, so ab⁻¹=e_G and a=b.
q_algebra_homomorphism_04.explanation: A homomorphism satisfies φ(e_G)=e_H. If injective, each g∈kerφ has φ(g)=φ(e_G), implying g=e_G. Conversely, if kerφ={e_G} and φ(a)=φ(b), then φ(ab⁻¹)=φ(a)φ(b)⁻¹=e_H. Thus ab⁻¹ is in the kernel and equals e_G, so a=b, proving injectivity.
q_algebra_homomorphism_04.grading_criteria: Prove both directions. In the converse construct ab⁻¹ correctly and use triviality of the kernel.

q_algebra_homomorphism_05.title: Distinguishing two integer maps as homomorphisms
q_algebra_homomorphism_05.statement: For maps from the integer additive group to itself, determine whether f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=2x are homomorphisms. Give reasons.
q_algebra_homomorphism_05.answer_text: f is not a homomorphism; g is.
q_algebra_homomorphism_05.explanation: A group homomorphism sends the additive identity 0 to 0, but f(0)=1, so f fails. Equivalently f(0+0)=1 differs from f(0)+f(0)=2. For g, g(x+y)=2(x+y)=2x+2y=g(x)+g(y), so it is a homomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_05.grading_criteria: Disprove the claim for f with a counterexample or the identity condition, and prove preservation for arbitrary x,y for g.

q_algebra_homomorphism_06.title: An isomorphism between additive and multiplicative groups
q_algebra_homomorphism_06.statement: Let U₅={1,2,3,4} under multiplication modulo 5. Prove φ:ℤ₄→U₅, φ([x]₄)=2ˣ(mod5), is a group isomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_06.answer_text: Since 2⁴≡1(mod5), the map is well-defined. Addition of exponents corresponds to multiplication of images. The images of 0,1,2,3 are 1,2,4,3, covering U₅ exactly once.
q_algebra_homomorphism_06.explanation: If x,y differ by 4k, then 2ˣ≡2ʸ(mod5) because 2⁴≡1. Negative exponents are interpreted using the inverse of 2 in U₅, so the class formula is well-defined. Also φ([x]+[y])=2^(x+y)=2ˣ2ʸ, preserving the operation. The four standard representatives have distinct images 1,2,4,3 covering U₅, hence φ is bijective and an isomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_06.grading_criteria: Include well-definedness, operation preservation, and verification of bijectivity from the four images.

q_algebra_homomorphism_07.title: When is modular reduction well-defined?
q_algebra_homomorphism_07.statement: Let m,n be positive integers. Prove φ([x]ₙ)=[x]ₘ defines a well-defined map ℤₙ→ℤₘ if and only if m∣n. When defined, show it preserves addition.
q_algebra_homomorphism_07.answer_text: It is well-defined exactly when m∣n. If n=mk, representatives differing by a multiple of n also differ by a multiple of m. Conversely [0]ₙ=[n]ₙ forces m∣n. Addition is preserved by adding representatives.
q_algebra_homomorphism_07.explanation: If m∣n, x≡y(modn) gives x−y=tn, divisible by m, so their image classes agree. Conversely well-definedness requires [0]ₙ and [n]ₙ to have the same image: [0]ₘ=[n]ₘ, giving m∣n. Under this condition φ([x]ₙ+[y]ₙ)=[x+y]ₘ=[x]ₘ+[y]ₘ, proving an additive homomorphism.
q_algebra_homomorphism_07.grading_criteria: Prove both directions of well-definedness and separately verify addition preservation.
